In about a week, Californians will be casting their ballots, and among the many initiatives is Proposition 38, which seeks to raise a lot of money for medical research. But beyond the measure itself, there is the broader political question of how the initiative process is being used to support private interests.
Proposition 38, if approved, would sell $8.4 billion in state bonds to raise funding specifically for immunology and immunotherapy research. It specifies that half the funding goes toward cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's research.
"And immunotherapies are the cutting-edge form of medical treatment that harness the body's own immune system to stop these diseases," said Yes on 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. "And so, this bond measure steps in and provides funding for this critical medical research, which is really important right now in the face of federal cuts."
That's the interest of Dr. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist who made his fortune inventing hundreds of surgical devices. But now he's interested in creating something new: a research facility at the former Westside Pavilion shopping mall near the University of California, Los Angeles, called the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
"It's the intention of this institute to have an internal, self-funded incubator accelerator to play 'Shark Tank,' if you will. We're going to have the world's leading immunologists and say, 'Yeah, let's invest in that and start a new company,'" Michelson said at a 2024 symposium about the institute which, at that point, existed only on paper.
"Right now, we are in the phase where we are raising funds," he said. "And philanthropy is one source of that. I really would like to find some business partners."
But it seems those business partners may now be the California taxpayers. Michelson's foundation has funded the campaign to the tune of about $40 million to get Prop. 38 on the ballot. And in the measure's language, it dedicates half the money - $4.2 billion - to a single "unnamed" non-profit. But the criteria for selecting that non-profit was written to exactly match Michelson's new institute, so no other entity in the state could possibly qualify.
Dr. Sarah Hill, political science professor at California State University, Fullerton, analyzes the state's voter initiatives and says bond money is usually reserved for long-lasting infrastructure projects because it incurs debt that lasts for decades.
"And it's bond money being used for research, which is kind of unusual," said Hill. "So, it's unusual policy, and you get this kind of unusual outcome as well, of one non-profit being eligible for half the money."
The other half of the money would be handed out in a traditional, competitive process for those applying for grants to study specific projects. But that wouldn't be the case for the CIII, which critics say would also be exempt from California's public disclosure laws. Servicing the bond debt is expected to take $500-600 million from the state's general fund for 20 years or more.
Dr. Robert Kaplan, a research senior scholar at Stanford University, is concerned that lawmakers will be reluctant to fund any other kinds of medical research when so much is going to only one field of study.
"One of the important things about science is that you need a lot of different people with different ideas," said Kaplan, who authored the opposition statement to the initiative. "And so, there's kind of a marketplace for ideas, where the best minds are competing with one another to get the research funding. And then, they're evaluated on their progress and only those who succeed are rewarded with continuing funding. And that model, there seems to be a lot of discussion in the scientific literature, but that model seems to be the best one."
Ulimately, Prop. 38 will be decided by the voters on the issue of curing disease, but it also may be ushering in a whole new way for those with big ideas and enough resources to use the ballot box to convince the public to pay to make them come true.
"And I think it just raises so many questions about this process. That, at this point in the process, is about who has the money to get it on the ballot and to push for it," Hill said. "It's frustrating to watch."
"That's exactly what you want people to spend their money on, which is curing cancer," said Swanson. "So, we're proud to have gotten funding in that way."
Supporters of Prop 38 say it could end up costing the taxpayer nothing because 10% of any profits from medical breakthroughs would be refunded back to the state. But Kaplan said those kind of monetary benefits are not guaranteed and usually take decades to be realized.

content.thinking:
This looks like a real 2026 initiative that has drawn a fair amount of press. I think the institute is tied to Gary Michelson, the billionaire spine surgeon and inventor who founded the Michelson Medical Research Foundation, and I recall the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII) at UCLA being announced under his backing.

I'm now looking at whether the Westside Pavilion building was bought by UCLA for its research park, which was meant to house the institute, and I'm recalling that the state budget set aside a large sum for that, possibly with Newsom's backing. Next I'll go through the law text and the news coverage, along with the campaign funding figures.

Should California borrow $8.4B for immunology research? Proposition 38 explained
By By Kiara Adams, video script produced using AI assistance
October 27, 2026 5:58 PM
Proposition 38 authorizes an $8.4 billion bond to support immunology and immunotherapy research following cuts from the Trump administration. Below is a transcript of the video above. Read our voter guide story on Prop. 38 here (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html), along with the editorial board’s take on the issue (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html).
$8.4 billion. That’s what California wants to borrow for medical research under Prop 38. Here’s the breakdown.
Proposition 38 asks voters to approve $8.4 billion in state borrowing (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317528464.html) for immunology and immunotherapy research — the science of how your immune system fights diseases like cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s. Like any bond measure, that money gets paid back over time, with interest, out of the state’s general fund.
Why now? Backers point to Trump administration cuts to federal funding for medical research (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html), which they say have left promising projects without funding. The Alzheimer’s Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation and the ALS Association are all on board.
But read the fine print. Half the money — $4.2 billion — is set aside for one nonprofit, and out of the state, critics say only one qualifies (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html): A UCLA institute backed by the proposition’s billionaire supporter, Gary Michaelson.
The price tag for taxpayers? Analysts estimate repayment at $500 to $600 million a year for roughly 20 years. Opponents call it “ballot-box science” — the idea that voters, not scientists or lawmakers, are choosing who gets funding. Supporters say patients can’t wait.
Voters have the final say on Nov. 3.

California Prop. 38 to use bond money to fund immunology research with half dedicated to one nonprofit
By

Add CBS News on Google (https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=cbsnews.com)
In about a week, Californians will be casting their ballots, and among the many initiatives is Proposition 38, which seeks to raise a lot of money for medical research. But beyond the measure itself, there is the broader political question of how the initiative process is being used to support private interests.
Proposition 38, if approved, would sell $8.4 billion in state bonds to raise funding specifically for immunology and immunotherapy research. It specifies that half the funding goes toward cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's research.
"And immunotherapies are the cutting-edge form of medical treatment that harness the body's own immune system to stop these diseases," said Yes on 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. "And so, this bond measure steps in and provides funding for this critical medical research, which is really important right now in the face of federal cuts."
That's the interest of Dr. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist who made his fortune inventing hundreds of surgical devices. But now he's interested in creating something new: a research facility at the former Westside Pavilion shopping mall near the University of California, Los Angeles, called the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
"It's the intention of this institute to have an internal, self-funded incubator accelerator to play 'Shark Tank,' if you will. We're going to have the world's leading immunologists and say, 'Yeah, let's invest in that and start a new company,'" Michelson said at a 2024 symposium about the institute which, at that point, existed only on paper.
"Right now, we are in the phase where we are raising funds," he said. "And philanthropy is one source of that. I really would like to find some business partners."
But it seems those business partners may now be the California taxpayers. Michelson's foundation has funded the campaign to the tune of about $40 million to get Prop. 38 on the ballot. And in the measure's language, it dedicates half the money - $4.2 billion - to a single "unnamed" non-profit. But the criteria for selecting that non-profit was written to exactly match Michelson's new institute, so no other entity in the state could possibly qualify.
Dr. Sarah Hill, political science professor at California State University, Fullerton, analyzes the state's voter initiatives and says bond money is usually reserved for long-lasting infrastructure projects because it incurs debt that lasts for decades.
"And it's bond money being used for research, which is kind of unusual," said Hill. "So, it's unusual policy, and you get this kind of unusual outcome as well, of one non-profit being eligible for half the money."
The other half of the money would be handed out in a traditional, competitive process for those applying for grants to study specific projects. But that wouldn't be the case for the CIII, which critics say would also be exempt from California's public disclosure laws. Servicing the bond debt is expected to take $500-600 million from the state's general fund for 20 years or more.
Dr. Robert Kaplan, a research senior scholar at Stanford University, is concerned that lawmakers will be reluctant to fund any other kinds of medical research when so much is going to only one field of study.
"One of the important things about science is that you need a lot of different people with different ideas," said Kaplan, who authored the opposition statement to the initiative. "And so, there's kind of a marketplace for ideas, where the best minds are competing with one another to get the research funding. And then, they're evaluated on their progress and only those who succeed are rewarded with continuing funding. And that model, there seems to be a lot of discussion in the scientific literature, but that model seems to be the best one."
Ulimately, Prop. 38 will be decided by the voters on the issue of curing disease, but it also may be ushering in a whole new way for those with big ideas and enough resources to use the ballot box to convince the public to pay to make them come true.
"And I think it just raises so many questions about this process. That, at this point in the process, is about who has the money to get it on the ballot and to push for it," Hill said. "It's frustrating to watch."
"That's exactly what you want people to spend their money on, which is curing cancer," said Swanson. "So, we're proud to have gotten funding in that way."
Supporters of Prop 38 say it could end up costing the taxpayer nothing because 10% of any profits from medical breakthroughs would be refunded back to the state. But Kaplan said those kind of monetary benefits are not guaranteed and usually take decades to be realized.

Determinations under this subparagraph shall be made
on a case-by-case basis, and, in any event, the
department shall not approve a royalty rate of less than

(2) Any agreement entered into by a recipient of

establishing a joint venture or other business
arrangement for the commercialization or monetization

recipient of research funds receives not less than 25
percent of the gross profits from that joint venture or
other business arrangement and any subsequent sale
of the joint venture or other business arrangement.
(g) Any institute, public or nonprofit university, or
nonprofit research institution that receives funding
pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 130352 shall
require all employees, scientists, researchers,
independent contractors, or other individuals receiving
funding via grant, contract, or otherwise from funds
originating under this chapter, who desire to publish the
results of research from that funding, to provide a copy
of the proposed written publication or an outline of an
oral disclosure to the institute, public or nonprofit
university, or nonprofit research institution for review at
least 30 days prior to any publication or presentation.
The reviewing institute, public or nonprofit university, or

both of the following:
(1) Propose modifications to the publication or
presentation for patent reasons or other reasons to be

presentation in order to protect patentable information
and allow patent applications protecting intellectual
property rights to be filed as determined by the
reviewing institute, public or nonprofit university, or
nonprofit research institution.
130359. (a) The institute shall issue an annual report
to the public that sets forth the institute’s activities,
research accomplishments, and the future direction of
the institute’s overall program.
(b) Each annual report shall include, but not be limited
to, all of the following:
(1) A summary of research findings, including
promising new research areas.
(2) A description of progress toward project goals and
key scientific findings or milestones.
(3) The number and type of peer-reviewed publications,
patents filed, or clinical trials initiated.
(4) A summary of the institute’s administrative
expenses.
(5) A report of the institute’s strategic research and
financial plans.
(c) The annual report shall be published on the
institute’s internet website.
130360. (a) The council shall issue an annual report
to the public that sets forth the grants awarded, grants
in progress, research accomplishments, and the future
direction of the council’s overall grant funding program.
(b) Each annual report shall include, but not be limited
to, all of the following:
(1) A summary of research findings by prior grantees,
including promising new research areas.
(2) The number and dollar amount of research grants
allocated that year.
(3) The grantees for the prior year and a report of their
research progress and accomplishments to date.
(4) An assessment of the relationship between the
council’s grants and the overall strategy of its research
program.
(5) A report of the council’s strategic research and
financial plans.
(6) A summary of the council’s administrative
expenses.
(c) The annual report shall be published on the
department’s internet website.

from a certified public accounting firm an independent
financial audit of its activities that shall be provided to
the Controller. The Controller shall review the audit and
annually issue a public report of that review. The

notice and a formal public comment period. The

more certified public accounting firms independent
financial audits of its activities and the activities of 10
percent of grantees, selected at random, that have
made expenditures with grant funding under this
chapter during the audit period. Those independent
financial audits shall be provided to the Controller, who
shall review the audits and annually issue a public
report of that review. The Controller shall hold a public
meeting with appropriate notice and a formal public
comment period. The Controller shall evaluate public
comments and shall include appropriate summaries in
the annual report.
130362. (a) (1) There shall be a Citizens’ Financial
Accountability Oversight Committee consisting of six
members.
(2) The California State Auditor, the Treasurer, the
President pro Tempore of the Senate, the Speaker of
the Assembly, and the chairperson of the council shall
each appoint a public member of the committee.
(3) The Controller, or the Controller’s designee, shall
serve as the chairperson of the committee.
(b) The committee shall do all of the following:
(1) Review the annual financial audits prepared
pursuant to Section 130361, the Controller’s reports on
those audits, and the financial practices of the institute
and the council.
(2) Issue an annual report that includes
recommendations on the financial practices and
performance of the institute and the council.
(3) Evaluate public comments and include appropriate
summaries in its annual report.
(c) The committee shall hold public meetings, with
appropriate notice, and with a formal public comment
period.
(d) The Controller shall furnish the committee with
staff support.

for any purpose under state law, including, but not

(commencing with Section 81000) of the Government

this section.
(1) A member of the council shall not make, participate
in making, or in any way attempt to use their official
position to influence a decision to approve or award a
grant or contract to their employer, but a member may
participate in a decision to approve or award a grant or
contract to an entity in the same field as their employer.
(2) A member of the council may participate in a
decision to approve or award a grant or contract to an
entity for the purpose of research involving a disease
from which the member or a person in their family
suffers.
(3) The adoption of general standards regarding
selection criteria and research priorities are not
decisions subject to conflict of interest prohibitions.

deemed to be inconsistent, incompatible, in conflict
with, or inimical to the duties of the council member as
a member of the faculty or administration of any system
of the University of California and shall not result in the
automatic vacation of either office.
(2) Service as a member of the council by a
representative or employee of a nonprofit academic or
research institution shall not be deemed to be
inconsistent, incompatible, in conflict with, or inimical
to the duties of the council member as a representative
or employee of that organization or institution.
(d) Section 1090 of the Government Code shall not
apply to any grant or contract made by the council
except where both of the following conditions are met:

making, participating in making, or in any way
attempting to use their official position to influence a
decision on the grant or contract.

Proposition 38 is a sleeper on the ballot. California voters should beware | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 24, 2026 2:20 PM
A laboratory technician works at a lab in Folsom in 2020. Proposition 38 would allow California to borrow $8.4 billion to support immunology research, half of which would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California.
DANIEL KIM
Sacramento Bee file
The search for medical interventions that can bolster our immune systems (https://www.niaid.nih.gov/research/immune-system-overview) to kill deadly diseases such as cancer is one of the most exciting fields in research. It’s why there is bipartisan support in Congress to spend roughly $2 billion annually in pursuit of cures once thought impossible.
Yet here in California, there is a proposed $8.4 billion bond on the ballot to fund immunology and immunotherapy research that is both too big and too flawed to seriously consider. Proposition 38 i (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html)s being underwritten by the backer of an institute affiliated with UCLA that wants to exempt itself from public-records laws.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html)
This is no way to invest public funds in research, and even if it were, no state can afford to replace the federal government’s role in primary research. California voters shouldn’t pretend otherwise. The collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/) Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urge a “No” vote on Prop. 38.
The National Institutes of Health funds 332 different (https://report.nih.gov/funding/categorical-spending#/) condition, research and disease categories. Prop. 38 asks Californians to fund a very narrow slice of the broader medical research spectrum. And it does so in a remarkably underhanded way.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) guarantees half the money to an institute tied to a campus healthcare system with a workload volume “greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year.”
That uniquely describes UCLA and an affiliated institution, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. (https://www.calimmunology.org/) It is backed by a billionaire physician and inventor, Gary K. Michelson. He is the money behind Prop. 38.
The institute’s web page boasts extraordinary goals — “to end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” But the public paper trail on this organization is thinner than ice.
Itslatest tax form reports (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093/202631219349301013/full) a fund balance of less than $20 million. The institute’s president reported to the Internal Revenue Service that his job required only two hours of work a week. And we’re supposed to trust this institute with $4.2 billion of our money?
It gets worse. Prop. 38 states: “The institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law …” This fine print is a bombshell.
It means we, the paying public, would learn precious little about how this institute operates. The California Public Records Act and other transparency laws would not apply. Today’s shell of an institute wants to become tomorrow’s billion-dollar black box.
Funding public research should not be a popularity contest. Immunology and immunotherapy are important, but so are countless other fields of medical research.
That is why it makes sense to maintain a national approach to health research rather than create a flavor-of-the-month club in California and other states. Whatever President Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk have done or said, a bipartisan coalition in Congress continues to fund federal research.
The leadership of the University of California system should be ashamed to be associated with such a secretive approach to conducting publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 is a sleeper on a crowded ballot, preying on Californians’ goodwill to spend billions that would otherwise go toward running the state. This measure is not a cure. It is a warm-and-fuzzy-sounding initiative designed to keep the public in the dark.

Proposition 38 is a sleeper on the ballot. California voters should beware | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 24, 2026 2:20 PM
A laboratory technician works at a lab in Folsom in 2020. Proposition 38 would allow California to borrow $8.4 billion to support immunology research, half of which would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California.
DANIEL KIM
Sacramento Bee file
The search for medical interventions that can bolster our immune systems (https://www.niaid.nih.gov/research/immune-system-overview) to kill deadly diseases such as cancer is one of the most exciting fields in research. It’s why there is bipartisan support in Congress to spend roughly $2 billion annually in pursuit of cures once thought impossible.
Yet here in California, there is a proposed $8.4 billion bond on the ballot to fund immunology and immunotherapy research that is both too big and too flawed to seriously consider. Proposition 38 i (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html)s being underwritten by the backer of an institute affiliated with UCLA that wants to exempt itself from public-records laws.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html)
This is no way to invest public funds in research, and even if it were, no state can afford to replace the federal government’s role in primary research. California voters shouldn’t pretend otherwise. The collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/) Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urge a “No” vote on Prop. 38.
The National Institutes of Health funds 332 different (https://report.nih.gov/funding/categorical-spending#/) condition, research and disease categories. Prop. 38 asks Californians to fund a very narrow slice of the broader medical research spectrum. And it does so in a remarkably underhanded way.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) guarantees half the money to an institute tied to a campus healthcare system with a workload volume “greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year.”
That uniquely describes UCLA and an affiliated institution, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. (https://www.calimmunology.org/) It is backed by a billionaire physician and inventor, Gary K. Michelson. He is the money behind Prop. 38.
The institute’s web page boasts extraordinary goals — “to end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” But the public paper trail on this organization is thinner than ice.
Itslatest tax form reports (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093/202631219349301013/full) a fund balance of less than $20 million. The institute’s president reported to the Internal Revenue Service that his job required only two hours of work a week. And we’re supposed to trust this institute with $4.2 billion of our money?
It gets worse. Prop. 38 states: “The institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law …” This fine print is a bombshell.
It means we, the paying public, would learn precious little about how this institute operates. The California Public Records Act and other transparency laws would not apply. Today’s shell of an institute wants to become tomorrow’s billion-dollar black box.
Funding public research should not be a popularity contest. Immunology and immunotherapy are important, but so are countless other fields of medical research.
That is why it makes sense to maintain a national approach to health research rather than create a flavor-of-the-month club in California and other states. Whatever President Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk have done or said, a bipartisan coalition in Congress continues to fund federal research.
The leadership of the University of California system should be ashamed to be associated with such a secretive approach to conducting publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 is a sleeper on a crowded ballot, preying on Californians’ goodwill to spend billions that would otherwise go toward running the state. This measure is not a cure. It is a warm-and-fuzzy-sounding initiative designed to keep the public in the dark.

Proposition 38 is a sleeper on the ballot. California voters should beware | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 24, 2026 2:20 PM
A laboratory technician works at a lab in Folsom in 2020. Proposition 38 would allow California to borrow $8.4 billion to support immunology research, half of which would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California.
DANIEL KIM
Sacramento Bee file
The search for medical interventions that can bolster our immune systems (https://www.niaid.nih.gov/research/immune-system-overview) to kill deadly diseases such as cancer is one of the most exciting fields in research. It’s why there is bipartisan support in Congress to spend roughly $2 billion annually in pursuit of cures once thought impossible.
Yet here in California, there is a proposed $8.4 billion bond on the ballot to fund immunology and immunotherapy research that is both too big and too flawed to seriously consider. Proposition 38 i (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html)s being underwritten by the backer of an institute affiliated with UCLA that wants to exempt itself from public-records laws.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html)
This is no way to invest public funds in research, and even if it were, no state can afford to replace the federal government’s role in primary research. California voters shouldn’t pretend otherwise. The collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/) Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urge a “No” vote on Prop. 38.
The National Institutes of Health funds 332 different (https://report.nih.gov/funding/categorical-spending#/) condition, research and disease categories. Prop. 38 asks Californians to fund a very narrow slice of the broader medical research spectrum. And it does so in a remarkably underhanded way.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) guarantees half the money to an institute tied to a campus healthcare system with a workload volume “greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year.”
That uniquely describes UCLA and an affiliated institution, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. (https://www.calimmunology.org/) It is backed by a billionaire physician and inventor, Gary K. Michelson. He is the money behind Prop. 38.
The institute’s web page boasts extraordinary goals — “to end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” But the public paper trail on this organization is thinner than ice.
Itslatest tax form reports (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093/202631219349301013/full) a fund balance of less than $20 million. The institute’s president reported to the Internal Revenue Service that his job required only two hours of work a week. And we’re supposed to trust this institute with $4.2 billion of our money?
It gets worse. Prop. 38 states: “The institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law …” This fine print is a bombshell.
It means we, the paying public, would learn precious little about how this institute operates. The California Public Records Act and other transparency laws would not apply. Today’s shell of an institute wants to become tomorrow’s billion-dollar black box.
Funding public research should not be a popularity contest. Immunology and immunotherapy are important, but so are countless other fields of medical research.
That is why it makes sense to maintain a national approach to health research rather than create a flavor-of-the-month club in California and other states. Whatever President Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk have done or said, a bipartisan coalition in Congress continues to fund federal research.
The leadership of the University of California system should be ashamed to be associated with such a secretive approach to conducting publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 is a sleeper on a crowded ballot, preying on Californians’ goodwill to spend billions that would otherwise go toward running the state. This measure is not a cure. It is a warm-and-fuzzy-sounding initiative designed to keep the public in the dark.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm noting the key terms of the bond measure: $8.4B in GO bonds, funded from the General Fund at roughly $500-600M a year for 20 years. Half of that, $4.2B, goes to one nonprofit institute whose criteria seem built around the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is tied to UCLA and backed by Gary Michelson. The text also says that institute won't be treated as a public agency under state law, which is the part I'm looking at next.

The bill then names the specific public records, open meeting, and political reform statutes the institute is exempt from, which seems to shield it from much of the usual state oversight. I'm also noticing that the timing of bond issuance hinges on a written request from the institute itself, giving it control over when the money flows.

I'm going through the rest of the bond measure's provisions: the institute's primary role in negotiating collaborative agreements, the five-year termination review, a $100 million General Fund start-up loan, and a 10% state share of IP revenue until the bonds are repaid. I'm also weighing the 20% discount for California purchasers, which could push companies away from licensing or raise national prices through Medicaid best-price rules.

I'm pulling in more coverage now: the LA Times, SF Chronicle, San Diego Union-Tribune, Mercury News, OC Register, CalMatters, and Hoover's Proposition Lab, plus the positions of groups like the Taxpayers Association, the League of Women Voters, and both state parties. I also want to check the Sacramento Bee piece about only one institute qualifying.

CALIFORNIA DECIDES | Proposition Lab
PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2038.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

Retired government analysts raise alarm on immunology bond on November ballot
By Tarini Mehta
September 11, 2026 3:33 PM
Ballots are dropped off at a polling location on Fountain Square Drive in Citrus Heights on Election Day, June 2, 2026.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Three former employees of the California Legislative Analyst’s Office came out in strong opposition against Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316259099.html) Thursday, arguing that the ballot measure that seeks to support medical research lacked appropriate provisions for transparency and accountability. Instead, they said, it seemed to “steer public funds” to its billionaire backer’s “philanthropic project” and then “hide its tracks.”
The proposition (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) will ask voters in the November election to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of medical research grants in recent months. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California appeared (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) to meet the criteria included in the measure for the nonprofit that would be awarded half the bond proceeds. That institute is the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Proposition 38.
‘Hides its tracks’
“Those of you who have worked with the Legislative Analyst’s Office before, you know how reticent our staff is to ever engage in partisan political debates,” said Marianne O’Malley, former managing principal analyst at the LAO, at a virtual news conference organized by the No on Proposition 38 campaign Thursday. “We don’t do that, so you may be wondering why three retired LAO staffers are talking publicly about Proposition 38. The reason is this is no ordinary measure. This measure hijacks the initiative process to steer public funds to a billionaire’s philanthropic project, and then it hides its tracks by waiving all the usual laws to promote governmental transparency.”
O’Malley said it is not uncommon for the government to transfer funds to a nonprofit or private entity to carry out a project. However, such a transfer usually follows an open and competitive bidding process — something Proposition 38 does not seem to do, she said.
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign, said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health.
Swanson said the measure was written to allocate funds to an institute that is “ready to go, competitive and world-class.” She said state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific nonprofit, but they can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open soon.
“We don’t have time to wait. Patients don’t have time to wait for another entity to be created,” Swanson said. “We want an institute that’s able to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.”
For O’Malley, the problem with the measure does not end with the selection of the institute. She said Proposition 38 did not have provisions to promote transparency after the money is disbursed. She pointed to a clause that said the chosen nonprofit institute was not to be deemed a public agency. Therefore, it would be immune from public records and open meeting requirements that ordinarily provide accountability over public funds.
Will it pay for itself?
The backers of Proposition 38 argue that it has strong accountability protections, including independent financial audits, annual reports, a citizens’ oversight committee and a 2% cap on state administrative costs, apart from the general transparency rules that all nonprofits must follow.
They also say the measure protects taxpayers and is designed to pay for itself, since 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the total costs of the bond. With the global immunotherapy market projected to grow rapidly over the next decade, supporters believe the research program created under Proposition 38 will create “more than enough revenue.” In addition, treatments developed through funded research are to be offered at a 20% discount in California.
However, Dan Carson, also a former LAO analyst, disputed that claim based on California’s experience with stem-cell research bonds passed in 2004 and 2020. In 2004, voters approved Proposition 71, creating the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine and authorizing $3 billion in bond funding for stem cell research. Californians approved an additional $5.5 billion for the institute in 2020.
During his time at the LAO, Carson said he worked on a team that analyzed Proposition 71 and found that it had failed to deliver on the huge financial windfall it had promised the state.
“The state eventually received only a tiny fraction of the billions of dollars we were promised,” he said. “We got about $16 million in payoff for intellectual property, and we were projected to spend about $6 billion over time to repay the principal and interest on those bonds. So here we go again with Prop. 38. This time, an even bigger $8.4 billion medical research bond issue that will cost us roughly half a billion dollars a year for decades to pay off.”
The research topics eligible for funding under the bond measure include understanding disease formation and factors that contribute to the same. While those research activities are important, Carson said, they do not directly develop new cures that can generate assets to pay off the bond costs. However, the measure does ask that projects with the “greatest potential for yielding the most immediate, accessible and affordable therapies” be prioritized in the competitive research grant selections.
Loading…
‘Institutional favoritism’
Those selections, for the half of the money that will not go to the single institute, will be made by a council consisting of representatives of the University of California campuses, nonprofit universities and research institutions in consultation with the selected institute. The grants will be awarded to universities and institutions represented on the council.
According to Judy Heiman, former principal analyst at the LAO, that creates a conflict of interest which will result in members of a closed group discussing how to divide up $4.2 billion amongst themselves rather than finding the best uses for the money.
“There’s a legitimate argument about whether California should add billions of dollars in medical research spending to its already substantial debt burden,” Heiman said. “Those who think we shouldn’t will vote against Prop. 38. I would argue that even those who would like to see a major state investment in research should vote no on Prop. 38 and demand an open, transparent and accountable structure. Scientific merit, not institutional favoritism, should drive where the money goes.”
The No on Proposition 38 campaign, led by Stanford Universitysenior scholar Robert Kaplan (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article315629674.html), has so far not reported any contributions. Kaplan has consistently criticized the practice of funding research focused on specific diseases rather than investing in medical research more broadly, especially when the Trump administration’s cuts affected public health programs across the board.
Support for Prop. 38
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $27 million so far, of which more than $22 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy.
The measure has the endorsement of the California Democratic Party and the California Republican Party. It is also supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association.
Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor whose life was saved by an immunotherapy clinical trial at UCLA, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California, but the country and the whole world.
“I lived through struggling to find new treatments for 12 years. I had heard about CAR T-cell therapy in 2012, but I had to wait six years for it to make it into trial because these things are not enough of a priority,” Adami said. “Everybody says the federal government will restore (research funding). I’m sorry, patients can’t wait for that, just like I couldn’t. If my trial hadn’t opened, I was a month away from dying. That’s how sick I was, and this is the case for too many people.”
In November, Prop. 38 will need “yes” votes from a majority of California voters to be approved.

PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2038.pdf)
Research

Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].

PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].

With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
