Endorsement: Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years
Proposition 38 on the November ballot authorizes the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy. But half of that money must go to an unnamed nonprofit medical research institute based on criteria that has no bearing on the ability to conduct high-quality, cutting-edge immunology research.
Daymond Gascon/S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 3, 2026
In a California election filled with compromised candidates and mind-numbing tax measures, wouldn’t it feel great to vote for something everyone can agree will make a positive difference in the world?
Proposition 38 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot positions itself as such a balm.
Opinion : This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/prop-38-california-newsom-22495203.php)
It would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy to identify treatments and cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease. If any drugs receive commercial approval, California patients would get a 20% discount off the national average price, and 10% of revenue would go to state coffers.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Who doesn’t want to cure cancer and save the state’s budget in the process?
But Prop 38 is no balm; it’s one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years.
The measure requires the California Department of Public Health to give half the bond money — $4.2 billion — to an unnamed nonprofit medical research institute that meets a long and unusual list of criteria, including occupying a minimum 200,000-square-foot space and receiving a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
These requirements have no bearing on an institution’s ability to conduct high-quality, cutting-edge immunology research. Instead, they’re written so that a lone research center is eligible to receive (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) the lion’s share of taxpayer money: the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California has many established and well-regarded research institutes — including some that have made significant advances in these fields.
But the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy is not among them.
Instead, it’s a brand-new institute, and its founders include the same billionaires who paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and financier Michael Milken, who, in addition to his longtime financing of medical research, (https://milkeninstitute.org/speakers/michael-milken-5) is also known as the “junk bond king.” He was pardoned by President Donald Trump in 2020 (https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/18/trump-pardons-michael-milken-face-of-1980s-financial-scandals.html) for his 1990 guilty plea to racketeering and securities fraud.
In an endorsement interview, Yes on 38 campaign spokesperson Robin Swanson insisted to us that the institute is “well positioned” to put $4.2 billion to good use, touting initial philanthropic contributions of $250 million (https://labusinessjournal.com/special-reports/bioscience-institute-takes-shape/#:~:text=Private%20donation%20commitments%20have%20totaled%20%24250%20million%20to%20date%2C%20primarily%20from%20the%20six%2Dmember%20board.) and its affiliation with UCLA and its medical center.
But the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy literally has no track record of developing, funding or bringing medical research to market. It isn’t even fully built. Despite already receiving $200 million in taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park) in California’s 2022-2023 budget (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2022-23/pdf/Enacted/BudgetSummary/HigherEducation.pdf), construction on a “majority” of the space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028, a spokesperson acknowledged via email.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Key leadership positions remain empty. As of this writing, the institute is still searching for a director, the spokesperson said.
It doesn’t even have a public strategic plan (https://www.calimmunology.org/about). When we pressed for details, the spokesperson would only say, “While CIII continues to refine its longer-term business plan, several core elements are complete or well underway.”
The spokesperson insisted that the institute wasn’t involved in drafting Prop 38 and isn’t part of the campaign. But, again, its billionaire co-founders put the measure on the ballot and have raised more than $38 million to support it (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
The institute may be playing coy about how it will benefit from Prop 38, but campaign proponents make no secret of where the money will end up.
“CIII is ready to go,” Swanson said, against all evidence.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Swanson and other Prop 38 supporters leaned heavily on the UCLA affiliation to assuage concerns over the institute’s glaring shortcomings.
UCLA is indeed a top research university. But what exactly is the “affiliation” here?
The institute is leasing space at a new UCLA Research Park (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) but will mostly operate independently from the university. An institute spokesperson said the “formal affiliation agreement” defines their “relationship and responsibilities,” including mission and purpose, facilities, funding, intellectual property, personnel and governance. Some senior UCLA leaders sit on the institute’s board of directors (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors), including Chancellor Julio Frenk, and UCLA “reserves the right to veto actions that it deems will result in reputational harm or contravene the university’s mission,” Phil Hampton, senior director of communications for UCLA Health and the David Geffen School of Medicine, said in an email.
These vague answers do not assuage our serious doubts about the institute’s ability to manage billions in taxpayer funds.
Indeed, the measure also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through Prop 38-funded research — even therapies created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Funding decisions would be made by a council of representatives from seven of the 10 University of California campuses — Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco — and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions.
But there are red flags here, as well.
The money is reserved for projects at the institutions represented on the council — raising serious conflict-of-interest concerns. (Proponents said council members would have to abide by ethics and conflict-of-interest regulations — although the measure carves out multiple exceptions — and the council and institute would be subject to independent audits and annual reporting requirements.)
Supporters ask voters to look past these issues by arguing that state-level investment is needed because of President Donald Trump’s funding cuts for medical research. But National Institutes of Health funding for immunotherapy research has steadily risen since 2019 (https://report.nih.gov/funding/categorical-spending#/), when it was established as a new category.
Moreover, Robert Kaplan, an opponent of the measure who was an associate director at the National Institutes of Health and formerly led UCLA’s health services program, told us that Prop 38 fundamentally misunderstands how funding top-tier medical research works.
It doesn’t make sense to restrict billions of dollars to just one area of research, Kaplan said. After all, there’s no guarantee that immunology, as opposed to another field of study, holds the cure to cancer or Alzheimer’s. Funding should be prioritized for thoroughly vetted projects that show the greatest promise of making a difference. Limiting the eligibility pool will almost certainly waste money on efforts that lack merit or scientific rigor.
That’s a lesson Californians should be familiar with.
In 2004, voters approved $3 billion in bonds for stem-cell research, swayed by the promise of miracle cures and huge financial windfalls for the state. Those didn’t materialize, a Chronicle investigation found (https://projects.sfchronicle.com/2018/stem-cells/politics/?_gl=1*76rb29*_gcl_aw*R0NMLjE3OTAxMTQ1MzUuQ2owS0NRand6c2pWQmhDM0FSSXNBTG5NdjRuS1U2OEx6Z3BLUndsckVzczNmZTNRNXlnVzNYeFI1VUprUDZqcXljR3h5SzFEQzg2QXBDSWFBa1RLRUFMd193Y0I.*_gcl_au*MTYxMzIzNzI3Mi4xNzg4OTExNzQ5*_ga*MTQ1MTQ5NDU3MS4xNzgxMTM0OTQ4*_ga_56G0ZT3ZD0*czE3OTA4MDgxMDkkbzExNCRnMSR0MTc5MDgwODg5MCRqNjAkbDAkaDA.); in fact, the measure may have actually empowered an uptick in clinics peddling pseudoscience.
That didn’t stop voters from approving yet another measure in 2020 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-Prop-14-no-need-to-15592513.php) authorizing $5.5 billion in bonds for stem-cell research.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
Let’s not make the same mistake a third time.
There isn’t a family in California who hasn’t been touched by cancer, Alzheimer’s or heart disease. Better treatments and cures cannot come fast enough. We applaud any billionaire who earnestly wants to harness their fortune to fight disease. But if Michelson, Luskin and Milken want Californians to believe that’s their intention with Prop 38, they should spend their own money and come back to taxpayers when their institute actually has some progress to show.

Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.

And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.

One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.

Why is it the best solution to that problem?
Prop. 38 makes a long-term investment in one of the most promising areas of medical science: immunology, which harnesses the body’s own immune system to prevent, treat and cure devastating diseases.
Immunotherapies are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Patients who have been weeks away from dying have received breakthrough treatments that have led to long-term remission.
Prop. 38 brings together California’s world-class universities, nonprofit research institutions and leading scientists in a statewide effort to accelerate breakthrough immunology research, while providing stable funding at a time when federal research dollars are shrinking and increasingly uncertain.
Prop. 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others.
Why should California taxpayers take on $8.4 billion in debt for medical research?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers. It requires 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies be returned to California to offset the full cost of the bond, including interest.
Prop. 38 mandates that new treatments and cures developed under Prop. 38 be offered to Californians at 20% below the national average.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term health care expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Public funding of medical research has always been a central component of advancements in medicine. Of new drugs approved by the FDA between 2010 and 2019, 99.4% were the result of publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 also includes strong accountability provisions such as annual audits and limiting state administrative costs to no more than 2%.
With the federal government and private companies already spending billions on medical research, why does California need to step in?
Billions in funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health and other federal partners are already putting critical research for cures at risk.
Private companies tend to invest where they see the clearest path to profit, which can leave promising but high-risk research underfunded — especially early-stage work, rare diseases and treatments that may take years to develop. Public investment is essential in filling that gap. It allows scientists to pursue breakthroughs based on scientific promise and medical need, not just commercial potential, and helps move discoveries far enough along to attract additional investment.
The fact is, those suffering from debilitating diseases can’t afford to wait for the market alone to deliver, or wait on the federal government to fund this research. California can continue to lead the way in breakthrough medical research and the development of cures with Prop. 38.
What happens if the research fails to find any new, profitable treatments?
The field of immunology and immunotherapies has already proved to be incredibly promising. Breakthrough immunotherapies have already been developed and approved to prevent and fight cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas, and more.
The global immunotherapy market was valued at about $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow rapidly, reaching $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.

This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).

Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)

It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.

Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.

Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.

And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.

This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)

It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.

And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 3:05 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:05 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.

Why is it the best solution to that problem?
Prop. 38 makes a long-term investment in one of the most promising areas of medical science: immunology, which harnesses the body’s own immune system to prevent, treat and cure devastating diseases.
Immunotherapies are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Patients who have been weeks away from dying have received breakthrough treatments that have led to long-term remission.
Prop. 38 brings together California’s world-class universities, nonprofit research institutions and leading scientists in a statewide effort to accelerate breakthrough immunology research, while providing stable funding at a time when federal research dollars are shrinking and increasingly uncertain.
Prop. 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others.
Why should California taxpayers take on $8.4 billion in debt for medical research?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers. It requires 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies be returned to California to offset the full cost of the bond, including interest.
Prop. 38 mandates that new treatments and cures developed under Prop. 38 be offered to Californians at 20% below the national average.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term health care expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Public funding of medical research has always been a central component of advancements in medicine. Of new drugs approved by the FDA between 2010 and 2019, 99.4% were the result of publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 also includes strong accountability provisions such as annual audits and limiting state administrative costs to no more than 2%.
With the federal government and private companies already spending billions on medical research, why does California need to step in?
Billions in funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health and other federal partners are already putting critical research for cures at risk.
Private companies tend to invest where they see the clearest path to profit, which can leave promising but high-risk research underfunded — especially early-stage work, rare diseases and treatments that may take years to develop. Public investment is essential in filling that gap. It allows scientists to pursue breakthroughs based on scientific promise and medical need, not just commercial potential, and helps move discoveries far enough along to attract additional investment.
The fact is, those suffering from debilitating diseases can’t afford to wait for the market alone to deliver, or wait on the federal government to fund this research. California can continue to lead the way in breakthrough medical research and the development of cures with Prop. 38.
What happens if the research fails to find any new, profitable treatments?
The field of immunology and immunotherapies has already proved to be incredibly promising. Breakthrough immunotherapies have already been developed and approved to prevent and fight cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas, and more.
The global immunotherapy market was valued at about $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow rapidly, reaching $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 3:05 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:05 PM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Why is it the best solution to that problem?
Prop. 38 makes a long-term investment in one of the most promising areas of medical science: immunology, which harnesses the body’s own immune system to prevent, treat and cure devastating diseases.
Immunotherapies are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Patients who have been weeks away from dying have received breakthrough treatments that have led to long-term remission.
Prop. 38 brings together California’s world-class universities, nonprofit research institutions and leading scientists in a statewide effort to accelerate breakthrough immunology research, while providing stable funding at a time when federal research dollars are shrinking and increasingly uncertain.
Prop. 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others.
Why should California taxpayers take on $8.4 billion in debt for medical research?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers. It requires 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies be returned to California to offset the full cost of the bond, including interest.
Prop. 38 mandates that new treatments and cures developed under Prop. 38 be offered to Californians at 20% below the national average.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term health care expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Public funding of medical research has always been a central component of advancements in medicine. Of new drugs approved by the FDA between 2010 and 2019, 99.4% were the result of publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 also includes strong accountability provisions such as annual audits and limiting state administrative costs to no more than 2%.
With the federal government and private companies already spending billions on medical research, why does California need to step in?
Billions in funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health and other federal partners are already putting critical research for cures at risk.
Private companies tend to invest where they see the clearest path to profit, which can leave promising but high-risk research underfunded — especially early-stage work, rare diseases and treatments that may take years to develop. Public investment is essential in filling that gap. It allows scientists to pursue breakthroughs based on scientific promise and medical need, not just commercial potential, and helps move discoveries far enough along to attract additional investment.
The fact is, those suffering from debilitating diseases can’t afford to wait for the market alone to deliver, or wait on the federal government to fund this research. California can continue to lead the way in breakthrough medical research and the development of cures with Prop. 38.
What happens if the research fails to find any new, profitable treatments?
The field of immunology and immunotherapies has already proved to be incredibly promising. Breakthrough immunotherapies have already been developed and approved to prevent and fight cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas, and more.
The global immunotherapy market was valued at about $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow rapidly, reaching $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.

This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.
About Opinion
Guest opinions in Open Forum and Insight are produced by writers with expertise, personal experience or original insights on a subject of interest to our readers. Their views do not necessarily reflect the opinion of The Chronicle editorial board, which is committed to providing a diversity of ideas to our readership.
Read more about our transparency and ethics policies (https://www.sfchronicle.com/standards/)
And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.
Emily Hoeven is a columnist and editorial writer for the Opinion section.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.

Why is it the best solution to that problem?
Prop. 38 makes a long-term investment in one of the most promising areas of medical science: immunology, which harnesses the body’s own immune system to prevent, treat and cure devastating diseases.
Immunotherapies are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Patients who have been weeks away from dying have received breakthrough treatments that have led to long-term remission.
Prop. 38 brings together California’s world-class universities, nonprofit research institutions and leading scientists in a statewide effort to accelerate breakthrough immunology research, while providing stable funding at a time when federal research dollars are shrinking and increasingly uncertain.
Prop. 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others.
Why should California taxpayers take on $8.4 billion in debt for medical research?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers. It requires 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies be returned to California to offset the full cost of the bond, including interest.
Prop. 38 mandates that new treatments and cures developed under Prop. 38 be offered to Californians at 20% below the national average.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term health care expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Public funding of medical research has always been a central component of advancements in medicine. Of new drugs approved by the FDA between 2010 and 2019, 99.4% were the result of publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 also includes strong accountability provisions such as annual audits and limiting state administrative costs to no more than 2%.
With the federal government and private companies already spending billions on medical research, why does California need to step in?
Billions in funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health and other federal partners are already putting critical research for cures at risk.
Private companies tend to invest where they see the clearest path to profit, which can leave promising but high-risk research underfunded — especially early-stage work, rare diseases and treatments that may take years to develop. Public investment is essential in filling that gap. It allows scientists to pursue breakthroughs based on scientific promise and medical need, not just commercial potential, and helps move discoveries far enough along to attract additional investment.
The fact is, those suffering from debilitating diseases can’t afford to wait for the market alone to deliver, or wait on the federal government to fund this research. California can continue to lead the way in breakthrough medical research and the development of cures with Prop. 38.
What happens if the research fails to find any new, profitable treatments?
The field of immunology and immunotherapies has already proved to be incredibly promising. Breakthrough immunotherapies have already been developed and approved to prevent and fight cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas, and more.
The global immunotherapy market was valued at about $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow rapidly, reaching $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.
