We believe California voters deserve a choice about investing in the future of scientific research and breakthroughs in our state. Prop. 38 puts that decision directly in the hands of voters, while requiring strong accountability for how the money is spent.
Prop. 38 provides the stable, long-term funding scientists need to pursue promising research without being dependent on changing political priorities or annual budget decisions, particularly as billions in federal research funding is being delayed and eliminated.
People who are living with debilitating diseases don’t have years to wait for the state or federal government to take action on this issue. We owe it to them to make this investment now by voting “yes” on Prop. 38.
What are the projected economic benefits and costs for lower-income households, small business owners and California taxpayers?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself. Ten percent of proceeds from licensing successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the cost of the bonds, including principal and interest.
The global immunotherapy market was already valued at approximately $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California, home to many of the world’s leading scientists and research institutions, to lead that rapidly growing field.
There are also potentially enormous savings from preventing and curing diseases that currently cost families and our healthcare system tens of billions of dollars.
Prop. 38 includes another important protection for Californians: treatments and technologies developed through this publicly funded research must be offered in California at prices at least 20% below the national average.
Californians are investing in the research, and they should share in its benefits.
Why should Californians lock up $500 million per year of their state’s General Fund because of a ballot initiative backed by a billionaire whose institute receives half of the bond money?
That characterization ignores both what Prop. 38 actually does and what Californians get in return. For starters, finding treatments and cures to the most debilitating and costly diseases will save billions in avoided health expenses.
Prop. 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs. Scientific research is an economic engine in California, and studies show that each dollar invested in medical research brings three dollars back into the economy.
And Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself while helping California lead a global immunotherapy market projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033.
The measure also contains strong taxpayer protections. Administrative costs are capped at 2%. Funds are tracked and audited. And 10% of licensing proceeds from successful therapies must be returned to California to help repay both the principal and interest on the bonds.
What proofs of concept is this ballot measure modeled on? When has California or another state achieved success with a similar plan?
We already know immunotherapy works. Breakthrough immunotherapies have been developed and approved to prevent and fight melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas and other cancers.
The opportunity now is to accelerate that progress and apply the science of the immune system to an even broader range of diseases.
Prop. 38 combines sustained funding with a statewide network so California’s leading scientists can collaborate, share sophisticated research infrastructure and move promising discoveries toward patients faster.
California has led medical innovation before. Prop. 38 gives us the opportunity to do it again.
Why restrict this to immunology rather than giving program managers more discretion, like DARPA does, to pick the most promising investments as evidence and trends reveal?
Immunology is already one of the most promising and rapidly advancing areas of medical science, with the potential to transform how we prevent and treat an enormous range of diseases.
Immunotherapy has already produced breakthrough treatments for cancers including melanoma, lung cancer, leukemia and lymphoma. Now scientists are exploring how the immune system can be harnessed against Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s and many other devastating conditions.
This is about investing in a broad scientific field that touches most of the diseases that kill and disable millions of Americans.
Prop. 38 gives qualified scientists and researchers the ability to determine which projects show the greatest scientific promise within that field.
And California is uniquely positioned to lead. We have many of the world’s leading universities, scientists and research institutions. Prop. 38 gives them the stable funding and shared infrastructure to turn scientific promise into treatments and cures.
What oversight mechanisms are in place to ensure the money is spent responsibly?
Prop. 38 limits state administrative costs to no more than 2%, requires all grant funds to public universities and nonprofit research centers be spent directly on medical research, implements rigorous conflict of interest rules, requires public disclosure of all spending, and mandates independent financial audits. Funds can only be granted to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes, and no funds can be given to for-profit corporations.
For the distribution of the competitive grants, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will organize a 7-member executive committee of appointees from the University of California campuses with the most qualified research facilities, including: Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco.
Additionally, treatments and technologies resulting from the research generally must be available here at prices at least 20% below the national average.
The bottom line is simple: Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on advancing research to save lives.
What do opponents get most wrong about this measure?
They lose sight of what Prop. 38 is actually about: saving lives.
Millions of Californians who are dealing with devastating diseases cannot afford to wait while promising medical research stalls because federal funding is being cut or because scientists lack the resources they need.
Prop. 38 creates a collaborative network of California universities, nonprofit research institutions and scientists focused on accelerating breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to save millions of lives.
It cultivates a world-class immunology research institute serving as a “hub” to foster collaboration among public universities, nonprofit research institutions and researchers. Requirements help ensure the institute is truly first-in-class globally, with the resources, expertise, staff, facilities, medical technology, information technology and access to clinical trials, patients and medical facilities to accelerate cures.
Prop. 38 will create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines competitive funding with a world-class institution designed to create cures that save lives.
What did we miss? What should we have asked you?
The impact on patients.
Imagine a new treatment that gives someone with cancer another decade with their family. An Alzheimer’s therapy that allows a parent to recognize their own children longer. Or a therapy that prevents a devastating disease before a family ever has to confront it.
That is the promise behind Prop. 38.
California is home to many of the greatest scientists, universities and research institutions in the world. Prop. 38 gives them stable, long-term funding and a statewide network to collaborate and move promising discoveries from the laboratory to patients faster.
That’s why leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others support Prop. 38.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
Why should Californians vote against funding research that could cure cancer or Alzheimer’s?
We strongly support biomedical research, including research on cancer and Alzheimer’s disease. The question is not whether the science is worthwhile, but whether Proposition 38 is a responsible way to fund it. It is not.
The measure would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, repayment would cost the General Fund more than $12 billion or about $500-600 million annually for 20 years. Those payments would compete with health care, education, public health, housing and other essential services.
Prop. 38 would also commit an extraordinary sum to immunology and immunotherapy while excluding hundreds of other important research priorities. California can support excellent science without allowing a ballot campaign to determine scientific priorities for a generation.

The state could potentially get a return on its investment through revenue sharing. Isn’t that a smart financial move?
The possibility of revenue isn’t a repayment plan. The promised financial return is uncertain in both size and timing. Prop. 38 requires 10% of revenue generated by funded discoveries to be returned to the state. Most basic discoveries, however, never become commercial products, and those that do commonly require years of additional research, clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing and private investment.
California’s experience with stem-cell research illustrates the risk of promising that research bonds will pay for themselves. The original stem-cell program authorized $3 billion in bonds, with a substantially larger repayment cost after interest. Its royalty returns have been modest relative to that public investment. Prop. 38 uses a different revenue-sharing formula, but speculative future income should not be treated as a dependable source of bond repayment.
The principal return from biomedical research is better health and scientific knowledge. Those benefits can be enormous, but they should not be confused with a guaranteed financial return to the state treasury.
We hope the research pays off — for patients and taxpayers alike. But a possible payoff isn’t a repayment plan.
Without this bond, how should California ensure it remains a leader in medical innovation?
California is already an international leader in biomedical research. In fiscal year 2025, four California institutions ranked among the nation’s 15 largest recipients among more than 2,500 institutions that receive National Institutes of Health funding: University of California, San Francisco, Stanford, UC San Diego and UCLA. University of Southern California, UC Davis, UC Irvine, Scripps Research, UC Berkeley and many other institutions also have exceptional research programs.
California should build on that strength through transparent, statewide competition. If the state chooses to supplement federal funding, it could create a broadly mandated research program that uses independent peer review, regularly reassesses priorities, and allows all qualified institutions and fields to compete. Scientific opportunities change rapidly; a sound funding system should be able to change with them.
Doesn’t the 20% discount on treatments provide a direct, tangible benefit to California residents?
A 20% discount would be welcome if an effective treatment emerged, but the provision is narrower and less certain than it sounds. It applies only to treatments resulting from Prop. 38-funded research and sold in California. Most funded projects will not produce a marketable therapy, and successful products could take many years to reach patients.
While the discount may sound attractive, forcing lower prices for California may incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled. The consequence could even be shortages in the state that developed the new approaches.
The measure also leaves unanswered questions about how the discount would be calculated, enforced and coordinated with insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, federal programs and confidential rebates. A promised discount on treatments that may never reach patients does not justify more than $8 billion in borrowing and decades of taxpayer repayments.
Twenty percent off an unknown price, for a treatment that may never arrive, is hardly a guarantee of affordable care.
How do you respond to the argument that federal funding cuts make state-level investments like this necessary?
The NIH has consistently enjoyed strong support from both Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. Congress. The president’s 2026-2027 budget included sharp cuts for the NIH and related research agencies. But Congress restored most of the funding. This is not to say we are satisfied with the federal outlook. We clearly support increased federal investment in biomedical research. Further, we find the politicization of the funding process unacceptable. Products of publicly funded research are available to anyone in any state or country. It is admirable that California might want to backfill some of the budget cuts. But, we feel, the costs should be shared equally among recipients of the benefit. That is why we believe in supporting a strong federal effort.
Medical breakthroughs benefit the whole country. Paying for them should be a shared national responsibility.

PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 3:39 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:06 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
Why should Californians vote against funding research that could cure cancer or Alzheimer’s?
We strongly support biomedical research, including research on cancer and Alzheimer’s disease. The question is not whether the science is worthwhile, but whether Proposition 38 is a responsible way to fund it. It is not.
The measure would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, repayment would cost the General Fund more than $12 billion or about $500-600 million annually for 20 years. Those payments would compete with health care, education, public health, housing and other essential services.
Prop. 38 would also commit an extraordinary sum to immunology and immunotherapy while excluding hundreds of other important research priorities. California can support excellent science without allowing a ballot campaign to determine scientific priorities for a generation.

The state could potentially get a return on its investment through revenue sharing. Isn’t that a smart financial move?
The possibility of revenue isn’t a repayment plan. The promised financial return is uncertain in both size and timing. Prop. 38 requires 10% of revenue generated by funded discoveries to be returned to the state. Most basic discoveries, however, never become commercial products, and those that do commonly require years of additional research, clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing and private investment.
California’s experience with stem-cell research illustrates the risk of promising that research bonds will pay for themselves. The original stem-cell program authorized $3 billion in bonds, with a substantially larger repayment cost after interest. Its royalty returns have been modest relative to that public investment. Prop. 38 uses a different revenue-sharing formula, but speculative future income should not be treated as a dependable source of bond repayment.
The principal return from biomedical research is better health and scientific knowledge. Those benefits can be enormous, but they should not be confused with a guaranteed financial return to the state treasury.
We hope the research pays off — for patients and taxpayers alike. But a possible payoff isn’t a repayment plan.
Without this bond, how should California ensure it remains a leader in medical innovation?
California is already an international leader in biomedical research. In fiscal year 2025, four California institutions ranked among the nation’s 15 largest recipients among more than 2,500 institutions that receive National Institutes of Health funding: University of California, San Francisco, Stanford, UC San Diego and UCLA. University of Southern California, UC Davis, UC Irvine, Scripps Research, UC Berkeley and many other institutions also have exceptional research programs.
California should build on that strength through transparent, statewide competition. If the state chooses to supplement federal funding, it could create a broadly mandated research program that uses independent peer review, regularly reassesses priorities, and allows all qualified institutions and fields to compete. Scientific opportunities change rapidly; a sound funding system should be able to change with them.
Doesn’t the 20% discount on treatments provide a direct, tangible benefit to California residents?
A 20% discount would be welcome if an effective treatment emerged, but the provision is narrower and less certain than it sounds. It applies only to treatments resulting from Prop. 38-funded research and sold in California. Most funded projects will not produce a marketable therapy, and successful products could take many years to reach patients.
While the discount may sound attractive, forcing lower prices for California may incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled. The consequence could even be shortages in the state that developed the new approaches.
The measure also leaves unanswered questions about how the discount would be calculated, enforced and coordinated with insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, federal programs and confidential rebates. A promised discount on treatments that may never reach patients does not justify more than $8 billion in borrowing and decades of taxpayer repayments.
Twenty percent off an unknown price, for a treatment that may never arrive, is hardly a guarantee of affordable care.
How do you respond to the argument that federal funding cuts make state-level investments like this necessary?
The NIH has consistently enjoyed strong support from both Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. Congress. The president’s 2026-2027 budget included sharp cuts for the NIH and related research agencies. But Congress restored most of the funding. This is not to say we are satisfied with the federal outlook. We clearly support increased federal investment in biomedical research. Further, we find the politicization of the funding process unacceptable. Products of publicly funded research are available to anyone in any state or country. It is admirable that California might want to backfill some of the budget cuts. But, we feel, the costs should be shared equally among recipients of the benefit. That is why we believe in supporting a strong federal effort.
Medical breakthroughs benefit the whole country. Paying for them should be a shared national responsibility.

PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 3:39 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:06 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
Why should Californians vote against funding research that could cure cancer or Alzheimer’s?
We strongly support biomedical research, including research on cancer and Alzheimer’s disease. The question is not whether the science is worthwhile, but whether Proposition 38 is a responsible way to fund it. It is not.
The measure would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, repayment would cost the General Fund more than $12 billion or about $500-600 million annually for 20 years. Those payments would compete with health care, education, public health, housing and other essential services.
Prop. 38 would also commit an extraordinary sum to immunology and immunotherapy while excluding hundreds of other important research priorities. California can support excellent science without allowing a ballot campaign to determine scientific priorities for a generation.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
The state could potentially get a return on its investment through revenue sharing. Isn’t that a smart financial move?
The possibility of revenue isn’t a repayment plan. The promised financial return is uncertain in both size and timing. Prop. 38 requires 10% of revenue generated by funded discoveries to be returned to the state. Most basic discoveries, however, never become commercial products, and those that do commonly require years of additional research, clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing and private investment.
California’s experience with stem-cell research illustrates the risk of promising that research bonds will pay for themselves. The original stem-cell program authorized $3 billion in bonds, with a substantially larger repayment cost after interest. Its royalty returns have been modest relative to that public investment. Prop. 38 uses a different revenue-sharing formula, but speculative future income should not be treated as a dependable source of bond repayment.
The principal return from biomedical research is better health and scientific knowledge. Those benefits can be enormous, but they should not be confused with a guaranteed financial return to the state treasury.
We hope the research pays off — for patients and taxpayers alike. But a possible payoff isn’t a repayment plan.
Without this bond, how should California ensure it remains a leader in medical innovation?
California is already an international leader in biomedical research. In fiscal year 2025, four California institutions ranked among the nation’s 15 largest recipients among more than 2,500 institutions that receive National Institutes of Health funding: University of California, San Francisco, Stanford, UC San Diego and UCLA. University of Southern California, UC Davis, UC Irvine, Scripps Research, UC Berkeley and many other institutions also have exceptional research programs.
California should build on that strength through transparent, statewide competition. If the state chooses to supplement federal funding, it could create a broadly mandated research program that uses independent peer review, regularly reassesses priorities, and allows all qualified institutions and fields to compete. Scientific opportunities change rapidly; a sound funding system should be able to change with them.
Doesn’t the 20% discount on treatments provide a direct, tangible benefit to California residents?
A 20% discount would be welcome if an effective treatment emerged, but the provision is narrower and less certain than it sounds. It applies only to treatments resulting from Prop. 38-funded research and sold in California. Most funded projects will not produce a marketable therapy, and successful products could take many years to reach patients.
While the discount may sound attractive, forcing lower prices for California may incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled. The consequence could even be shortages in the state that developed the new approaches.
The measure also leaves unanswered questions about how the discount would be calculated, enforced and coordinated with insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, federal programs and confidential rebates. A promised discount on treatments that may never reach patients does not justify more than $8 billion in borrowing and decades of taxpayer repayments.
Twenty percent off an unknown price, for a treatment that may never arrive, is hardly a guarantee of affordable care.
How do you respond to the argument that federal funding cuts make state-level investments like this necessary?
The NIH has consistently enjoyed strong support from both Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. Congress. The president’s 2026-2027 budget included sharp cuts for the NIH and related research agencies. But Congress restored most of the funding. This is not to say we are satisfied with the federal outlook. We clearly support increased federal investment in biomedical research. Further, we find the politicization of the funding process unacceptable. Products of publicly funded research are available to anyone in any state or country. It is admirable that California might want to backfill some of the budget cuts. But, we feel, the costs should be shared equally among recipients of the benefit. That is why we believe in supporting a strong federal effort.
Medical breakthroughs benefit the whole country. Paying for them should be a shared national responsibility.

We believe California voters deserve a choice about investing in the future of scientific research and breakthroughs in our state. Prop. 38 puts that decision directly in the hands of voters, while requiring strong accountability for how the money is spent.
Prop. 38 provides the stable, long-term funding scientists need to pursue promising research without being dependent on changing political priorities or annual budget decisions, particularly as billions in federal research funding is being delayed and eliminated.
People who are living with debilitating diseases don’t have years to wait for the state or federal government to take action on this issue. We owe it to them to make this investment now by voting “yes” on Prop. 38.
What are the projected economic benefits and costs for lower-income households, small business owners and California taxpayers?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself. Ten percent of proceeds from licensing successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the cost of the bonds, including principal and interest.
The global immunotherapy market was already valued at approximately $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California, home to many of the world’s leading scientists and research institutions, to lead that rapidly growing field.
There are also potentially enormous savings from preventing and curing diseases that currently cost families and our healthcare system tens of billions of dollars.
Prop. 38 includes another important protection for Californians: treatments and technologies developed through this publicly funded research must be offered in California at prices at least 20% below the national average.
Californians are investing in the research, and they should share in its benefits.
Why should Californians lock up $500 million per year of their state’s General Fund because of a ballot initiative backed by a billionaire whose institute receives half of the bond money?
That characterization ignores both what Prop. 38 actually does and what Californians get in return. For starters, finding treatments and cures to the most debilitating and costly diseases will save billions in avoided health expenses.
Prop. 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs. Scientific research is an economic engine in California, and studies show that each dollar invested in medical research brings three dollars back into the economy.
And Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself while helping California lead a global immunotherapy market projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033.
The measure also contains strong taxpayer protections. Administrative costs are capped at 2%. Funds are tracked and audited. And 10% of licensing proceeds from successful therapies must be returned to California to help repay both the principal and interest on the bonds.
What proofs of concept is this ballot measure modeled on? When has California or another state achieved success with a similar plan?
We already know immunotherapy works. Breakthrough immunotherapies have been developed and approved to prevent and fight melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas and other cancers.
The opportunity now is to accelerate that progress and apply the science of the immune system to an even broader range of diseases.
Prop. 38 combines sustained funding with a statewide network so California’s leading scientists can collaborate, share sophisticated research infrastructure and move promising discoveries toward patients faster.
California has led medical innovation before. Prop. 38 gives us the opportunity to do it again.
Why restrict this to immunology rather than giving program managers more discretion, like DARPA does, to pick the most promising investments as evidence and trends reveal?
Immunology is already one of the most promising and rapidly advancing areas of medical science, with the potential to transform how we prevent and treat an enormous range of diseases.
Immunotherapy has already produced breakthrough treatments for cancers including melanoma, lung cancer, leukemia and lymphoma. Now scientists are exploring how the immune system can be harnessed against Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s and many other devastating conditions.
This is about investing in a broad scientific field that touches most of the diseases that kill and disable millions of Americans.
Prop. 38 gives qualified scientists and researchers the ability to determine which projects show the greatest scientific promise within that field.
And California is uniquely positioned to lead. We have many of the world’s leading universities, scientists and research institutions. Prop. 38 gives them the stable funding and shared infrastructure to turn scientific promise into treatments and cures.
What oversight mechanisms are in place to ensure the money is spent responsibly?
Prop. 38 limits state administrative costs to no more than 2%, requires all grant funds to public universities and nonprofit research centers be spent directly on medical research, implements rigorous conflict of interest rules, requires public disclosure of all spending, and mandates independent financial audits. Funds can only be granted to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes, and no funds can be given to for-profit corporations.
For the distribution of the competitive grants, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will organize a 7-member executive committee of appointees from the University of California campuses with the most qualified research facilities, including: Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco.
Additionally, treatments and technologies resulting from the research generally must be available here at prices at least 20% below the national average.
The bottom line is simple: Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on advancing research to save lives.
What do opponents get most wrong about this measure?
They lose sight of what Prop. 38 is actually about: saving lives.
Millions of Californians who are dealing with devastating diseases cannot afford to wait while promising medical research stalls because federal funding is being cut or because scientists lack the resources they need.
Prop. 38 creates a collaborative network of California universities, nonprofit research institutions and scientists focused on accelerating breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to save millions of lives.
It cultivates a world-class immunology research institute serving as a “hub” to foster collaboration among public universities, nonprofit research institutions and researchers. Requirements help ensure the institute is truly first-in-class globally, with the resources, expertise, staff, facilities, medical technology, information technology and access to clinical trials, patients and medical facilities to accelerate cures.
Prop. 38 will create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines competitive funding with a world-class institution designed to create cures that save lives.
What did we miss? What should we have asked you?
The impact on patients.
Imagine a new treatment that gives someone with cancer another decade with their family. An Alzheimer’s therapy that allows a parent to recognize their own children longer. Or a therapy that prevents a devastating disease before a family ever has to confront it.
That is the promise behind Prop. 38.
California is home to many of the greatest scientists, universities and research institutions in the world. Prop. 38 gives them stable, long-term funding and a statewide network to collaborate and move promising discoveries from the laboratory to patients faster.
That’s why leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others support Prop. 38.

Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
Why should Californians vote against funding research that could cure cancer or Alzheimer’s?
We strongly support biomedical research, including research on cancer and Alzheimer’s disease. The question is not whether the science is worthwhile, but whether Proposition 38 is a responsible way to fund it. It is not.
The measure would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, repayment would cost the General Fund more than $12 billion or about $500-600 million annually for 20 years. Those payments would compete with health care, education, public health, housing and other essential services.
Prop. 38 would also commit an extraordinary sum to immunology and immunotherapy while excluding hundreds of other important research priorities. California can support excellent science without allowing a ballot campaign to determine scientific priorities for a generation.

The state could potentially get a return on its investment through revenue sharing. Isn’t that a smart financial move?
The possibility of revenue isn’t a repayment plan. The promised financial return is uncertain in both size and timing. Prop. 38 requires 10% of revenue generated by funded discoveries to be returned to the state. Most basic discoveries, however, never become commercial products, and those that do commonly require years of additional research, clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing and private investment.
California’s experience with stem-cell research illustrates the risk of promising that research bonds will pay for themselves. The original stem-cell program authorized $3 billion in bonds, with a substantially larger repayment cost after interest. Its royalty returns have been modest relative to that public investment. Prop. 38 uses a different revenue-sharing formula, but speculative future income should not be treated as a dependable source of bond repayment.
The principal return from biomedical research is better health and scientific knowledge. Those benefits can be enormous, but they should not be confused with a guaranteed financial return to the state treasury.
We hope the research pays off — for patients and taxpayers alike. But a possible payoff isn’t a repayment plan.
Without this bond, how should California ensure it remains a leader in medical innovation?
California is already an international leader in biomedical research. In fiscal year 2025, four California institutions ranked among the nation’s 15 largest recipients among more than 2,500 institutions that receive National Institutes of Health funding: University of California, San Francisco, Stanford, UC San Diego and UCLA. University of Southern California, UC Davis, UC Irvine, Scripps Research, UC Berkeley and many other institutions also have exceptional research programs.
California should build on that strength through transparent, statewide competition. If the state chooses to supplement federal funding, it could create a broadly mandated research program that uses independent peer review, regularly reassesses priorities, and allows all qualified institutions and fields to compete. Scientific opportunities change rapidly; a sound funding system should be able to change with them.
Doesn’t the 20% discount on treatments provide a direct, tangible benefit to California residents?

It applies only to treatments resulting from Prop. 38-funded research and sold in California. Most funded projects will not produce a marketable therapy, and successful products could take many years to reach patients.
While the discount may sound attractive, forcing lower prices for California may incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled. The consequence could even be shortages in the state that developed the new approaches.
The measure also leaves unanswered questions about how the discount would be calculated, enforced and coordinated with insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, federal programs and confidential rebates. Twenty percent off an unknown price, for a treatment that may never arrive, is hardly a guarantee of affordable care.

The president’s 2026-2027 budget included sharp cuts for the NIH and related research agencies. But Congress restored most of the funding. That is why we believe in supporting a strong federal effort.

This story is part of California Voices, a commentary forum aiming to broaden our understanding of the state and spotlight Californians directly impacted by policy or its absence. Learn more here (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/). Three decades ago, as the 20 th century was winding down, a culture war erupted over the use of human embryos (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2744932/) in researching stem cell cures for dreaded diseases. It was a subset of the nation’s never-ending conflict over abortion. After Republican George W. Bush won the presidency in 2000 his administration barred the use of embryos in genetic research, a policy President Barack Obama later revoked. In 2004, Robert Klein, a wealthy Bay Area real estate developer whose son suffered from Type 1 diabetes, launched a campaign to stimulate genetic research in California that didn’t rely on federal funds. Actors Michael J. Fox and Christopher Reeve, who were dealing with their own chronic medical conditions, starred in ads promoting Proposition 71 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_71,_Stem_Cell_Research_Initiative_(2004)), a 2004 ballot measure creating the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/). The measure also authorized $3 billion in bonds that the new state agency would distribute to research projects. Klein contributed heavily to the Prop. 71 campaign, raised money from others and served as the first chairman of the agency’s board. The campaign’s pitch to voters was not only that dread diseases would be cured but that California would reap the economic benefits of taking the lead. Voters endorsed the measure over the opposition of religious anti-abortion groups, and the agency began awarding grants to researchers, many of whom had ties to members of the new agency’s board of directors. ELECTION 2026 (https://calmatters.org/tag/election-2026) 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know Over the ensuing years it has touted several successes, but there has been no independent analysis of results. As the initial $3 billion was running out, advocates wrote a 2020 ballot measure, Proposition 14 (https://calmatters.org/health/2020/10/prop-14-stem-cell-research-funding/), that authorized another $5.5 billion in bonds. It won voter approval. Now the willingness of California voters to again float bonds for medical research underlies Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. And it raises questions about whether its sponsors would have the inside track for its $8.4 billion in proposed bond money. CalMatters delved into the very specific language of the measure and determined that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, founded and headed by billionaire Gary Michelson, would be the only organization that would qualify for half of the money (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/). Michelson is one of the major backers of Prop. 38. The other half of the bond issue would be distributed as grants to research applicants by a new council selected by representatives of seven University of California campuses, and each grant recipient will be linked to a member of the council. At this juncture, it’s important voters understand something about state general obligation bonds: They are not free money, even if sponsors often imply that they are. Bonds are loans from banks and other investors and, like all loans, must be repaid with interest. The Legislative Analyst’s Office has estimated the state budget would have to appropriate about $500 million a year for 25 years (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250488.pdf) to service Prop. 38’s bonds, or about $12.5 billion total. Bond repayments have the highest legal priority in the budget, so they displace funds that could otherwise be spent on education, healthcare or other services. Issuing bonds to support one avenue of medical research is a questionable activity regardless of cost. If the state has a legitimate role to play in such research, all potential fields should be explored, not merely pet projects and organizations that some billionaire patrons have chosen to the exclusion of others. Nevertheless, immunology is not the last field that voters will be asked to support. Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed new legislation, Senate Bill 895 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb895), that creates another new agency to award scientific research grants, the California Foundation for Science and Health Research. The measure places a $7.5 billion bond issue on the 2028 ballot to provide the new foundation with funds to distribute. This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready?
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)
October 20, 2026 5:00 am
Share on X (Opens in new window)

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
Mazziotta also told the regents the institute’s construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.
Institute would be exempt from public records act
CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. The council would generally (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=The%20Political%20Reform%20Act%20of%201974%20(Title%209%20(commencing%20with%20Section%2081000)%20of%20the%20Government%20Code)%20shall%20apply%20to%20the%20council%2C%20except%20as%20provided%20in%20this%20section.) be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing.
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure.
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed (https://yeson38.com/newsroom/press-releases/) Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. The union doesn’t represent faculty.
Money raised in support of Prop. 38 now exceeds $66 million, including at least $61.2 million in contributions from Michelson and his policy institute. Roughly $14 million of that includes loans from Michelson. The no camp has raised about $8,800

The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
Mazziotta also told the regents the institute’s construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.

CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. The council would generally (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=The%20Political%20Reform%20Act%20of%201974%20(Title%209%20(commencing%20with%20Section%2081000)%20of%20the%20Government%20Code)%20shall%20apply%20to%20the%20council%2C%20except%20as%20provided%20in%20this%20section.) be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing.
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure.
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed (https://yeson38.com/newsroom/press-releases/) Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. The union doesn’t represent faculty.

The council would generally (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=The%20Political%20Reform%20Act%20of%201974%20(Title%209%20(commencing%20with%20Section%2081000)%20of%20the%20Government%20Code)%20shall%20apply%20to%20the%20council%2C%20except%20as%20provided%20in%20this%20section.) be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing.
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure.
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed (https://yeson38.com/newsroom/press-releases/) Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. The union doesn’t represent faculty.

Fox and Christopher Reeve, who were dealing with their own chronic medical conditions, starred in ads promoting Proposition 71 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_71,_Stem_Cell_Research_Initiative_(2004)), a 2004 ballot measure creating the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/). The measure also authorized $3 billion in bonds that the new state agency would distribute to research projects. The campaign’s pitch to voters was not only that dread diseases would be cured but that California would reap the economic benefits of taking the lead. As the initial $3 billion was running out, advocates wrote a 2020 ballot measure, Proposition 14 (https://calmatters.org/health/2020/10/prop-14-stem-cell-research-funding/), that authorized another $5.5 billion in bonds. It won voter approval. Now the willingness of California voters to again float bonds for medical research underlies Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. And it raises questions about whether its sponsors would have the inside track for its $8.4 billion in proposed bond money. CalMatters delved into the very specific language of the measure and determined that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, founded and headed by billionaire Gary Michelson, would be the only organization that would qualify for half of the money (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/). Michelson is one of the major backers of Prop. 38. The other half of the bond issue would be distributed as grants to research applicants by a new council selected by representatives of seven University of California campuses, and each grant recipient will be linked to a member of the council. At this juncture, it’s important voters understand something about state general obligation bonds: They are not free money, even if sponsors often imply that they are. Bonds are loans from banks and other investors and, like all loans, must be repaid with interest. The Legislative Analyst’s Office has estimated the state budget would have to appropriate about $500 million a year for 25 years (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250488.pdf) to service Prop. 38’s bonds, or about $12.5 billion total. Bond repayments have the highest legal priority in the budget, so they displace funds that could otherwise be spent on education, healthcare or other services. Issuing bonds to support one avenue of medical research is a questionable activity regardless of cost. If the state has a legitimate role to play in such research, all potential fields should be explored, not merely pet projects and organizations that some billionaire patrons have chosen to the exclusion of others. Nevertheless, immunology is not the last field that voters will be asked to support. Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed new legislation, Senate Bill 895 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb895), that creates another new agency to award scientific research grants, the California Foundation for Science and Health Research. The measure places a $7.5 billion bond issue on the 2028 ballot to provide the new foundation with funds to distribute. CalMatters delved into the very specific language of the measure and determined that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, founded and headed by billionaire Gary Michelson, would be the only organization that would qualify for half of the money (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/). Michelson is one of the major backers of Prop. 38. The other half of the bond issue would be distributed as grants to research applicants by a new council selected by representatives of seven University of California campuses, and each grant recipient will be linked to a member of the council. At this juncture, it’s important voters understand something about state general obligation bonds: They are not free money, even if sponsors often imply that they are. Bonds are loans from banks and other investors and, like all loans, must be repaid with interest. The Legislative Analyst’s Office has estimated the state budget would have to appropriate about $500 million a year for 25 years (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250488.pdf) to service Prop. 38’s bonds, or about $12.5 billion total. Bond repayments have the highest legal priority in the budget, so they displace funds that could otherwise be spent on education, healthcare or other services. Issuing bonds to support one avenue of medical research is a questionable activity regardless of cost. If the state has a legitimate role to play in such research, all potential fields should be explored, not merely pet projects and organizations that some billionaire patrons have chosen to the exclusion of others. Nevertheless, immunology is not the last field that voters will be asked to support. Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed new legislation, Senate Bill 895 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb895), that creates another new agency to award scientific research grants, the California Foundation for Science and Health Research. The measure places a $7.5 billion bond issue on the 2028 ballot to provide the new foundation with funds to distribute. Prop 38 asks: Should California take on more debt to fund a single field of medical research?

By Dan Walters, CalMatters

This commentary was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

Three decades ago, as the 20th century was winding down, a culture war erupted over the use of human embryos in researching stem cell cures for dreaded diseases.

It was a subset of the nation’s never-ending conflict over abortion. After Republican George W. Bush won the presidency in 2000 his administration barred the use of embryos in genetic research, a policy President Barack Obama later revoked.

In 2004, Robert Klein, a wealthy Bay Area real estate developer whose son suffered from Type 1 diabetes, launched a campaign to stimulate genetic research in California that didn’t rely on federal funds.

Actors Michael J. Fox and Christopher Reeve, who were dealing with their own chronic medical conditions, starred in ads promoting Proposition 71, a 2004 ballot measure creating the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine. The measure also authorized $3 billion in bonds that the new state agency would distribute to research projects.

Klein contributed heavily to the Prop. 71 campaign, raised money from others and served as the first chairman of the agency’s board. The campaign’s pitch to voters was not only that dread diseases would be cured but that California would reap the economic benefits of taking the lead.

Voters endorsed the measure over the opposition of religious anti-abortion groups, and the agency began awarding grants to researchers, many of whom had ties to members of the new agency's board of directors.

Over the ensuing years it has touted several successes, but there has been no independent analysis of results. As the initial $3 billion was running out, advocates wrote a 2020 ballot measure, Proposition 14, that authorized another $5.5 billion in bonds. It won voter approval.

This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready?
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)
October 20, 2026 5:00 am
Share on X (Opens in new window)
