This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.
Mazziotta also told the regents the institute’s construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.
Institute would be exempt from public records act
CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. The council would generally (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=The%20Political%20Reform%20Act%20of%201974%20(Title%209%20(commencing%20with%20Section%2081000)%20of%20the%20Government%20Code)%20shall%20apply%20to%20the%20council%2C%20except%20as%20provided%20in%20this%20section.) be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing.
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure.
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed (https://yeson38.com/newsroom/press-releases/) Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The union of graduate students and post-doctoral researchers, whose pay often relies on science research funding, has also endorsed the proposition. The union doesn’t represent faculty.
Money raised in support of Prop. 38 now exceeds $66 million, including at least $61.2 million in contributions from Michelson and his policy institute. Roughly $14 million of that includes loans from Michelson. The no camp has raised about $8,800

Three decades ago, as the 20 th century was winding down, a culture war erupted over the use of human embryos (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2744932/) in researching stem cell cures for dreaded diseases. It was a subset of the nation’s never-ending conflict over abortion. After Republican George W. Bush won the presidency in 2000 his administration barred the use of embryos in genetic research, a policy President Barack Obama later revoked. In 2004, Robert Klein, a wealthy Bay Area real estate developer whose son suffered from Type 1 diabetes, launched a campaign to stimulate genetic research in California that didn’t rely on federal funds. Actors Michael J. Fox and Christopher Reeve, who were dealing with their own chronic medical conditions, starred in ads promoting Proposition 71 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_71,_Stem_Cell_Research_Initiative_(2004)), a 2004 ballot measure creating the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine (https://www.cirm.ca.gov/). The measure also authorized $3 billion in bonds that the new state agency would distribute to research projects. Klein contributed heavily to the Prop. 71 campaign, raised money from others and served as the first chairman of the agency’s board. The campaign’s pitch to voters was not only that dread diseases would be cured but that California would reap the economic benefits of taking the lead. Voters endorsed the measure over the opposition of religious anti-abortion groups, and the agency began awarding grants to researchers, many of whom had ties to members of the new agency’s board of directors. As the initial $3 billion was running out, advocates wrote a 2020 ballot measure, Proposition 14 (https://calmatters.org/health/2020/10/prop-14-stem-cell-research-funding/), that authorized another $5.5 billion in bonds. It won voter approval. Now the willingness of California voters to again float bonds for medical research underlies Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. And it raises questions about whether its sponsors would have the inside track for its $8.4 billion in proposed bond money. CalMatters delved into the very specific language of the measure and determined that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, founded and headed by billionaire Gary Michelson, would be the only organization that would qualify for half of the money (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/). Michelson is one of the major backers of Prop. 38. The other half of the bond issue would be distributed as grants to research applicants by a new council selected by representatives of seven University of California campuses, and each grant recipient will be linked to a member of the council. At this juncture, it’s important voters understand something about state general obligation bonds: They are not free money, even if sponsors often imply that they are. Bonds are loans from banks and other investors and, like all loans, must be repaid with interest. The Legislative Analyst’s Office has estimated the state budget would have to appropriate about $500 million a year for 25 years (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250488.pdf) to service Prop. 38’s bonds, or about $12.5 billion total. Bond repayments have the highest legal priority in the budget, so they displace funds that could otherwise be spent on education, healthcare or other services. Issuing bonds to support one avenue of medical research is a questionable activity regardless of cost. If the state has a legitimate role to play in such research, all potential fields should be explored, not merely pet projects and organizations that some billionaire patrons have chosen to the exclusion of others. Nevertheless, immunology is not the last field that voters will be asked to support. Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed new legislation, Senate Bill 895 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb895), that creates another new agency to award scientific research grants, the California Foundation for Science and Health Research. The measure places a $7.5 billion bond issue on the 2028 ballot to provide the new foundation with funds to distribute. Now I'm weighing the counterarguments: half the money going to a single institute built around one partner, with few staff and no director yet, plus its exemption from public records and open meetings rules, and the grant council drawn from the institutions that would receive the grants.

#### BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it.
It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years.
Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
- **Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research.** Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure.

The initiative would fund immunology and immunotherapy research aimed at harnessing the body’s immune system to develop new treatments, medical procedures and potential cures for diseases such as cancer, Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease.

Additionally, Prop 38 would make it mandatory for the state to enter into an agreement with a qualified nonprofit institute focused and dedicated to researching immunology and immunotherapy within 90 days of the initiative’s effective date.

California voters will decide in November whether Proposition (Prop) 38 should authorize substantial state funding for immunology and immunotherapy research.
The initiative would fund immunology and immunotherapy research aimed at harnessing the body’s immune system to develop new treatments, medical procedures and potential cures for diseases such as cancer, Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease.
More specifically, Prop 38, **titled the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative**, is split into three main components that would go into effect if passed.
First, the initiative would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds to support immunology and immunotherapy research.
At least half of the bond proceeds, or $4.2 billion, would be dedicated exclusively to research.
Additionally, Prop 38 would make it mandatory for the state to enter into an agreement with a qualified nonprofit institute focused and dedicated to researching immunology and immunotherapy within 90 days of the initiative’s effective date.
The research institute must be affiliated with the University of California.

I've got enough on the critiques, so now I'm turning to the case in favor, starting with immunology and immunotherapy and how federal research funding cuts add instability. Patient advocacy groups back it too, and I'm noting the governor and the state Democratic Party as supporters as well.

Now I'm weighing the counterarguments: half the money going to a single institute built around one partner, with few staff and no director yet, plus its exemption from public records and open meetings rules, and the grant council drawn from the institutions that would receive the grants.

Next I'm checking which major newspapers have opposed the measure, and whether the LA Times has weighed in at all this cycle. I also want to see where the Orange County Register, the Press Democrat, and the League of Women Voters and taxpayer groups stand, along with any UC position and the latest PPIC poll.

#### BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it.
It would authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for about 20 years.
Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays for schools, health care, and other public services.
- **Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research.** Bonds are best suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure.

- **Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to come.** About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.

Election Countdown
11 days until the November election
We’ve gone over a lot of ballot props. That includes:
The wealth tax, or Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), and its countermeasures (https://voiceofsandiego.org/2026/10/09/how-to-make-sense-of-the-major-tax-propositions-on-the-ballot/), Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) and Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/)
Prop. 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), the initiative to change how California recalls officials (https://voiceofsandiego.org/2026/10/16/should-california-change-how-it-does-recall-elections/) and
Another proposal, Prop. 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/), to lift a ban that prohibits political candidates from financing their campaigns with public dollars.
This week, we’ll break down three bond measures on the ballot, which, if voters approve, would add a collective $45 billion before interest to the state’s debt for biomedical research, housing construction and home loans.
What to Know About Prop. 38
University budgets were rocked last year after the Trump administration slashed hundreds of federal research grants.
While much of that funding has been restored, the uncertainty left institutions cautious and looking to find alternative ways to fund research. An $8.4 billion bond to subsidize immunotherapy research to fight cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease could help address this, say backers of Prop. 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/).

Half of the money would go to a single University of California-affiliated institute, while the remaining $4.2 billion would be doled out to other select nonprofit and research organizations.
Any medications developed from research supported by the bond funding would have to be sold at a 20 percent discount to Californians and 10 percent of any revenue would go back to the state’s coffers.
Surgeon and billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson put it on the ballot. Medical groups such as the American Association of Immunologists are supporters, and Alzheimer’s San Diego said it is backing Prop. 38 because it’d more quickly provide treatment research to the nearly 100,000 people in the county living with Alzheimer’s or dementia. San Diego County Democrats also endorsed the measure.
The League of Women Voters and Stanford researcher and former National Institute of Health Director Robert Kaplan oppose it, arguing that billions of dollars for years to come shouldn’t just be for one field of health research.
Critics have also increasingly questioned why a single nonprofit would receive half the bond money. CalMatters’ reporting (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) showed that Michelson’s own institute, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, would be the beneficiary.
Michelson is Prop. 38’s primary financier, contributing $61 million of the Yes campaign’s $66 million total. Opponents have raised $9,000.
What to Know About Prop. 1 and Prop. 37, the Other Megabonds
The end is near in our bond measure journey. Here’s the quick and dirty run-down:
Voting yes on Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) would mean California could borrow $11.25 billion for all kinds of affordable housing programs, from rentals to student dormitories, to veteran and farmworker housing.
Democrats in the Legislature put this one on the ballot, and it’s backed by the governor and statewide apartment association who say it’ll spur much-needed building to address California’s homelessness and affordability crisis.
Some Republicans, including San Diego GOP Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), are not feeling it. He and others argue it would do little to make housing more affordable while taxpayers will be left on the hook.
Its cousin, Prop. 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), would create a loan program to allow private lenders to give up to 17 percent of the cost of a newly built home to would-be buyers. It’d do this by allowing the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in bonds.
A coalition of real estate and labor groups put the measure on the ballot, and SEIU and the California Association of Realtors are its bankrollers. They argue that in a state where the median home price is $900,000 (https://carorg.sharepoint.com/:x:/s/CAR-RE-PublicProducts/IQAK-pU7cef4QpkWsCPlxwZKAbdKLa3OO0vFwHpuH_FADK8?rtime=7Fo4fkkx30g), it’d create a pathway for middle-class families to enter into homeownership.
But … but … but …
Doesn’t that mean taking on even more debt?
Yes, critics such as the League of Women Voters say. They think it’s not a good idea to let people buy homes they otherwise can’t afford by allowing buyers to go deeper into debt.
Unconventional Alliances
Things get curious if we zoom-in on Prop.38’s backers and naysayers.
Take the California Democratic Party, to which Michelson is a longtime donor. The Los Angeles-based philanthropist physician has given more than $100,000 to Democrats this cycle alone. That includes at least $25,0000 to Xavier Becerra in his campaign for governor as well as nearly $80,000 to fellow Angeleno Antonio Villaraigosa for his failed gubernatorial bid. He’s also donated to Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/robert-rivas-165041)’ re-election campaign.
Michelson has spread his fortune in San Diego, too. In 2020, he gave Assemblymember Tasha Boerner (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tasha-boerner-horvath-165421) $4,700 for her re-election campaign, and labor leader and former Assemblymember Lorena Gonzalez received thousands of dollars from Michelson for her 2020 re-election campaign. Two years later, he gave more than $10,000 to her brief, unsuccessful run for secretary of state.
The California GOP has endorsed Prop. 38, while choosing to stay neutral on Prop. 1, the $11 billion bond to build more affordable housing, and Prop. 37, the $25 billion bond to help finance new homeowners’ mortgages. DeMaio also supports the immunology research bond, saying in a podcast episode (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/videos/ca-voter-guide-yes-to-prop-38-no-on-prop-44) that it’s a better deal for taxpayers than to most other loans because therapies developed with the funding would be sold at a discount to consumers. He is against the two housing bonds.
Meanwhile, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association opposes all three bond measures, which they call an inappropriate use of public funds. They argue that biomedical research should be financed by pharmaceutical companies or the federal government rather than California residents.
They’re in company with the League of Women Voters who similarly argue that Prop. 38 is a misappropriation of public dollars, and that such funding shouldn’t be directed toward one UC-affiliated nonprofit.
Plenty of state lawmakers from the San Diego area didn’t want to wade in on this one, though, with one notable exception.
In a statement, San Diego Assemblymember Chris Ward (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/christopher-ward-35497) said he’s against the research bond because the funding would go to the one institution rather than to other California researchers who are best positioned to find cures and deliver treatments. He supports the housing bonds.
Getting responses from other Democrats, meanwhile, proved difficult.
Derek Humphrey, a campaign spokesperson for Boerner, said she doesn’t take public positions on propositions because she believes voters should weigh in on them, not their elected officials.
Chula Vista Assemblymember David Alvarez (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/david-alvarez-112993) is still undecided about the research bond, campaign manager Chris Jonsmyr said, but he supports both of the housing measures.
Campaign manager Skyler Johnson did not respond to emails asking if Encinitas state Sen. Catherine Blakespear supports or opposes Prop. 38, nor did Jeremy Addis-Mills, campaign manager for state Sen. Akilah Weber Pierson .

PROP 1 VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS SUPPORT
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and
there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years
for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading
to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide
safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction,
acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for
homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for
veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be
repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
Vote YES on Proposition 1
PROP 2 SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT SUPPORT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so
it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies
heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are
profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments.
These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that
revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a
larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are
2
unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions,
natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad
years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget
actions.
Vote YES on Proposition 2
PROP 3 CHILDREN'S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION SUPPORT
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services
by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of
taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an
estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate
today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest
helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public
services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while
schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3
simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The
League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California
weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
Vote YES on Proposition 3
PROP 4 CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT SUPPORT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big
donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates
without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while
candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on
public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create
voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no
campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and
how to design and pay for it.
3
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without
personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to
voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests,
these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian
American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our
population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the
state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose
candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more
reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and
agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety
cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public
funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a
campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in
California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters
have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.
Vote YES on Proposition 4
(The LWVC is an official proponent and has signed ballot arguments.)
PROP 5 RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS SUPPORT
California's recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never
become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a
small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today's recall rules allow, since the
same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets
the most votes, even if that's far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an
officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by
whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and
with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can
easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the
leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of
recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
4
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should
remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the
replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy
is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority
support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A
recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too - the
choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is
any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat
by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while
ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.
Vote YES on Proposition 5
(The LWVC is an official proponent and has signed ballot arguments.)
PROP 37 LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OPPOSE
OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families.
The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades
and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and
homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second
mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
• Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep.
Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their
first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would
not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the
program.
• The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting
families facing the greatest barriers. Generations of housing discrimination have
left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives
no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or
former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income
could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers
would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
• The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for
5
newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near
jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation,
insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
• Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether
investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other
assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or
purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront
racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not
meet that test.
Vote NO on Proposition 37
PROP 38 BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH OPPOSE
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would
authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and
require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for
about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays
for schools, health care, and other public services.
• Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best
suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With
interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent
more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
• Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to
come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research
institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved
for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and
public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those
changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a
ballot measure.
• Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters
approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties
and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in
its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to
research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative
Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
6
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to
decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do
the most good.
Vote NO on Proposition 38
PROP 39 PROHIBITS VOTING WITHOUT OPPOSE
GOVERNMENT-ISSUED ID
Prop 39 is a partisan power grab to further President Trump’s voter suppression efforts.
It is based on lies about our elections. Prop 39 is intended to make it harder to vote and
easier for politicians to decide which voters count. Right-wing billionaires spent millions
to put it on the ballot.
• California's elections are already secure. Voters swear to citizenship under
penalty of perjury, and officials verify identity at registration, check the rolls in
person, and match every mail ballot signature.
• A new registration hurdle. Millions of existing voters could be forced to
effectively re-register to “designate” a government ID for mail voting, like a
driver's license or Social Security number.
• Identity theft risk. You would be required to put the last four digits of that
sensitive ID number on the outside of your ballot envelope – next to your name,
address, and signature.
• Valid ballots thrown out. Your mailed ballot would not be counted if the number
you wrote didn’t match the “designated” number. One wrong digit or a blank field
could sink a valid ballot, with no guaranteed notice or chance to fix it. Texas tried
this and rejected one in eight mail ballots. Those voters were less likely to vote
again.
• An ID check every time you vote in person. You would have to show a
government-issued ID every time, even after officials verified who you are. Most
voters turned away under similar laws elsewhere had qualifying ID, just not on
them.
• A modern-day poll tax. A “free” ID is not free. Getting one costs transportation,
childcare, time off work, and fees for the paperwork behind it. Seniors, students,
low-income workers, voters with disabilities, and voters of color are hit hardest.
• Valid ID still must match. Nearly 30 percent of U.S. adults have changed their
name, 94 percent of them women. Californians who took a new name at marriage,
and transgender voters whose documents lag may hold valid ID and be turned
away anyway.
7
• Bad data and wrongful purges. Citizenship checks would likely run through
untrustworthy federal databases that wrongly flag eligible citizens to purge them
from voter rolls.
• Longer lines and slower results. Extra ID checks and flagged ballots add delay,
and the lawsuits would stretch it further, handing election deniers more time to
spread lies.
• Hundreds of millions of dollars every year. New systems, staffing, free ID cards,
audits, and lawsuits, all paid for while California already has budget problems.
Don't let President Trump and right-wing billionaires decide whose vote counts.
Vote NO on Proposition 39
(The LWVC is an official opponent and has signed ballot arguments.)
PROP 40 BILLIONAIRE TAX NEUTRAL
Prop 40 would tax extreme wealth to help meet urgent needs, but its one-time structure
conflicts with principles of sound public finance and risks long-term revenue loss.
The federal government is walking away from feeding people and providing access to
basic health care, putting Medi-Cal coverage and CalFresh benefits at risk for millions of
Californians. When it does, the state has a responsibility to step in. Prop 40 would
impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on billionaire wealth. The state would direct 90% of
the revenue to health care, with the remaining 10% going to education, food assistance,
and administration of the wealth tax. That could deliver tens of billions to the safety net
when families are losing both.
The measure also confronts a deeper problem the League cannot ignore. The wealthiest
American households pay a lower total effective tax rate than the whole population,
largely because business wealth produces little taxable income. As of September 2025,
roughly 900 American billionaires held nearly double the wealth of the entire bottom
half of the country. Inequality on that scale demands that solutions like wealth taxes get
serious consideration.
On the con side, Prop 40 makes budget decisions at the ballot box, locking the proceeds
into an earmarked fund. The Legislature could choose how to spend within those
categories but could not redirect the money to other needs. A one-time tax is also only a
stopgap for programs that need funding every year. Furthermore, the tax rests on only a
few hundred people. Of these, six billionaires reportedly left the state before the January
1, 2026, cutoff, potentially erasing more than one-quarter of the proponents’ projected
8
$100 billion revenue. It should be noted that the government estimates only tens of
billions of dollars raised over several years and says the amount is highly uncertain. The
government also estimates that state revenue could be reduced by less than $1 billion
per year.
The deeper fear is behavioral: that the tax pushes billionaires out after they pay and
deters others from ever coming. The government offers only the broad estimate that
state revenue could be reduced by below $1 billion per year. On the other hand, some
research finds that tax-driven migration among the wealthy is modest, and Silicon
Valley's ecosystem is not easily traded away.
The human need is urgent and asking those most able to pay to fill a hole the federal
government created is a fair demand. But the tax mechanism limits legislative flexibility
for allocating money where it is most crucial and raises the risk of taxpayer flight.
Because we have strong positions on both sides of this measure, the League takes a
neutral position on Prop 40.
PROP 41 LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES & REQUIRES SPECIAL TAX AUDITS OPPOSE
Prop 41 would put revenue from new state taxes under the Gann Limit’s rigid
constitutional spending cap, making it harder to fund essential services and respond to
changing needs. It would apply to any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after
January 1, 2026.
The League opposed the Gann Initiative in 1979 because its spending limit was too
inflexible to assure adequate government services in an uncertain future. Prop 41 would
extend that constraint to new tax revenue. This is especially concerning for voter-
approved initiatives, which generally cannot be changed by the Legislature without
another vote of the people.
Prop 41 would also require audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes,
including programs such as public campaign financing that may not receive General Fund
support. If a new tax excluded its revenue from the Gann Limit, the state could not
impose, collect, or enforce it. And when the state is at or near the limit, Prop 41 could
prevent all the revenue voters approved for a specific purpose from being spent on that
purpose.
The audits would add state costs, estimated by the Legislative Analyst’s Office in the low
millions of dollars annually and growing over time. The General Fund would pay for a
9
pre-election audit if an initiative failed to qualify or is rejected by voters. New programs
could also be difficult to evaluate before they exist.
Prop 41 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both
Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 41 pass and Prop 41 receives more “yes”
votes, courts could find that they conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming law.
Litigation could delay a final determination.
Vote NO on Proposition 41
PROP 42 LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES ON PERSONAL PROPERTY OPPOSE
Prop 42 would lock broad new restrictions on state taxing power into the California
Constitution, limiting California’s ability to respond to future needs.
• The ban goes far beyond retirement savings. It would prohibit new state taxes on
the ownership or control of a wide range of personal property, including stocks
and other financial assets, business interests, art, intellectual property, retirement
accounts, and other savings and assets.
• Prop 42 would limit certain retroactive state taxes. This includes new taxes
based on conduct, activity, or status that occurred before the tax took effect.
• The restrictions would be difficult to change. Because they would be in the
Constitution, changing them in the future would require another vote of the
people. A tax that does not make sense today may be appropriate under different
circumstances in the future.
Prop 42 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both
Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 42 pass and Prop 42 receives more “yes”
votes, courts could find that the measures conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming

Election Countdown
11 days until the November election
We’ve gone over a lot of ballot props. That includes:
The wealth tax, or Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), and its countermeasures (https://voiceofsandiego.org/2026/10/09/how-to-make-sense-of-the-major-tax-propositions-on-the-ballot/), Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) and Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/)
Prop. 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), the initiative to change how California recalls officials (https://voiceofsandiego.org/2026/10/16/should-california-change-how-it-does-recall-elections/) and
Another proposal, Prop. 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/), to lift a ban that prohibits political candidates from financing their campaigns with public dollars.
This week, we’ll break down three bond measures on the ballot, which, if voters approve, would add a collective $45 billion before interest to the state’s debt for biomedical research, housing construction and home loans.
What to Know About Prop. 38
University budgets were rocked last year after the Trump administration slashed hundreds of federal research grants.
While much of that funding has been restored, the uncertainty left institutions cautious and looking to find alternative ways to fund research. An $8.4 billion bond to subsidize immunotherapy research to fight cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease could help address this, say backers of Prop. 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/).

Any medications developed from research supported by the bond funding would have to be sold at a 20 percent discount to Californians and 10 percent of any revenue would go back to the state’s coffers.
Surgeon and billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson put it on the ballot. Medical groups such as the American Association of Immunologists are supporters, and Alzheimer’s San Diego said it is backing Prop. 38 because it’d more quickly provide treatment research to the nearly 100,000 people in the county living with Alzheimer’s or dementia. The League of Women Voters and Stanford researcher and former National Institute of Health Director Robert Kaplan oppose it, arguing that billions of dollars for years to come shouldn’t just be for one field of health research.
Critics have also increasingly questioned why a single nonprofit would receive half the bond money. CalMatters’ reporting (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) showed that Michelson’s own institute, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, would be the beneficiary.

Voting yes on Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) would mean California could borrow $11.25 billion for all kinds of affordable housing programs, from rentals to student dormitories, to veteran and farmworker housing.
Democrats in the Legislature put this one on the ballot, and it’s backed by the governor and statewide apartment association who say it’ll spur much-needed building to address California’s homelessness and affordability crisis.
Some Republicans, including San Diego GOP Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), are not feeling it. He and others argue it would do little to make housing more affordable while taxpayers will be left on the hook.
Its cousin, Prop. 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), would create a loan program to allow private lenders to give up to 17 percent of the cost of a newly built home to would-be buyers. it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies
heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are
profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments.
These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that
revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a
larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are
2
unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions,
natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad
years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget
actions.
Vote YES on Proposition 2
PROP 3 CHILDREN'S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION SUPPORT
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services
by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of
taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an
estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate
today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest
helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public
services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while
schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3
simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The
League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California
weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
Vote YES on Proposition 3
PROP 4 CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT SUPPORT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big
donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates
without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while
candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on
public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create
voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no
campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and
how to design and pay for it.
3
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without
personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to
voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests,
these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian
American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our
population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the
state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose
candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more
reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and
agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety
cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public
funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a
campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in
California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters
have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.
Vote YES on Proposition 4

PROP 5 RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS SUPPORT
California's recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never
become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a
small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today's recall rules allow, since the
same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets
the most votes, even if that's far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an
officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by
whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and
with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can
easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the
leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of
recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
4
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should
remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the
replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy
is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority
support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A
recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too - the
choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is
any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat
by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while
ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.

PROP 38 BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH OPPOSE
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would
authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and
require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for
about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays
for schools, health care, and other public services.
• Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best
suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With
interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent
more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.

come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research
institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved
for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and
public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those
changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a
ballot measure.

approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties

its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to
research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative
Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
6
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to
decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do
the most good.

PROP 40 BILLIONAIRE TAX NEUTRAL
Prop 40 would tax extreme wealth to help meet urgent needs, but its one-time structure
conflicts with principles of sound public finance and risks long-term revenue loss.
The federal government is walking away from feeding people and providing access to
basic health care, putting Medi-Cal coverage and CalFresh benefits at risk for millions of
Californians. When it does, the state has a responsibility to step in. Prop 40 would
impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on billionaire wealth. The state would direct 90% of
the revenue to health care, with the remaining 10% going to education, food assistance,
and administration of the wealth tax. That could deliver tens of billions to the safety net
when families are losing both.
The measure also confronts a deeper problem the League cannot ignore. The wealthiest
American households pay a lower total effective tax rate than the whole population,
largely because business wealth produces little taxable income. As of September 2025,
roughly 900 American billionaires held nearly double the wealth of the entire bottom
half of the country. Inequality on that scale demands that solutions like wealth taxes get
serious consideration.
On the con side, Prop 40 makes budget decisions at the ballot box, locking the proceeds
into an earmarked fund. The Legislature could choose how to spend within those
categories but could not redirect the money to other needs. A one-time tax is also only a
stopgap for programs that need funding every year. Furthermore, the tax rests on only a
few hundred people. Of these, six billionaires reportedly left the state before the January
1, 2026, cutoff, potentially erasing more than one-quarter of the proponents’ projected
8
$100 billion revenue. It should be noted that the government estimates only tens of
billions of dollars raised over several years and says the amount is highly uncertain. The
government also estimates that state revenue could be reduced by less than $1 billion
per year.
The deeper fear is behavioral: that the tax pushes billionaires out after they pay and
deters others from ever coming. The government offers only the broad estimate that
state revenue could be reduced by below $1 billion per year. On the other hand, some
research finds that tax-driven migration among the wealthy is modest, and Silicon
Valley's ecosystem is not easily traded away.
The human need is urgent and asking those most able to pay to fill a hole the federal
government created is a fair demand. But the tax mechanism limits legislative flexibility
for allocating money where it is most crucial and raises the risk of taxpayer flight.
Because we have strong positions on both sides of this measure, the League takes a
neutral position on Prop 40.
PROP 41 LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES & REQUIRES SPECIAL TAX AUDITS OPPOSE
Prop 41 would put revenue from new state taxes under the Gann Limit’s rigid
constitutional spending cap, making it harder to fund essential services and respond to
changing needs. It would apply to any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after
January 1, 2026.
The League opposed the Gann Initiative in 1979 because its spending limit was too
inflexible to assure adequate government services in an uncertain future. Prop 41 would
extend that constraint to new tax revenue. This is especially concerning for voter-
approved initiatives, which generally cannot be changed by the Legislature without
another vote of the people.
Prop 41 would also require audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes,
including programs such as public campaign financing that may not receive General Fund
support. If a new tax excluded its revenue from the Gann Limit, the state could not
impose, collect, or enforce it. And when the state is at or near the limit, Prop 41 could
prevent all the revenue voters approved for a specific purpose from being spent on that
purpose.
The audits would add state costs, estimated by the Legislative Analyst’s Office in the low
millions of dollars annually and growing over time. The General Fund would pay for a
9
pre-election audit if an initiative failed to qualify or is rejected by voters. New programs
could also be difficult to evaluate before they exist.
Prop 41 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both
Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 41 pass and Prop 41 receives more “yes”
votes, courts could find that they conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming law.
Litigation could delay a final determination.
Vote NO on Proposition 41

government also estimates that state revenue could be reduced by less than $1 billion
per year.
The deeper fear is behavioral: that the tax pushes billionaires out after they pay and
deters others from ever coming. The government offers only the broad estimate that
state revenue could be reduced by below $1 billion per year. On the other hand, some
research finds that tax-driven migration among the wealthy is modest, and Silicon
Valley's ecosystem is not easily traded away.
The human need is urgent and asking those most able to pay to fill a hole the federal
government created is a fair demand. But the tax mechanism limits legislative flexibility
for allocating money where it is most crucial and raises the risk of taxpayer flight.
Because we have strong positions on both sides of this measure, the League takes a
neutral position on Prop 40.
PROP 41 LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES & REQUIRES SPECIAL TAX AUDITS OPPOSE
Prop 41 would put revenue from new state taxes under the Gann Limit’s rigid
constitutional spending cap, making it harder to fund essential services and respond to
changing needs. It would apply to any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after
January 1, 2026.
The League opposed the Gann Initiative in 1979 because its spending limit was too
inflexible to assure adequate government services in an uncertain future. Prop 41 would
extend that constraint to new tax revenue. This is especially concerning for voter-
approved initiatives, which generally cannot be changed by the Legislature without
another vote of the people.
Prop 41 would also require audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes,
including programs such as public campaign financing that may not receive General Fund
support. If a new tax excluded its revenue from the Gann Limit, the state could not
impose, collect, or enforce it. And when the state is at or near the limit, Prop 41 could
prevent all the revenue voters approved for a specific purpose from being spent on that
purpose.
The audits would add state costs, estimated by the Legislative Analyst’s Office in the low
millions of dollars annually and growing over time. The General Fund would pay for a
9
pre-election audit if an initiative failed to qualify or is rejected by voters. New programs
could also be difficult to evaluate before they exist.
Prop 41 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both
Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 41 pass and Prop 41 receives more “yes”
votes, courts could find that they conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming law.
Litigation could delay a final determination.
Vote NO on Proposition 41
PROP 42 LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES ON PERSONAL PROPERTY OPPOSE
Prop 42 would lock broad new restrictions on state taxing power into the California
Constitution, limiting California’s ability to respond to future needs.
• The ban goes far beyond retirement savings. It would prohibit new state taxes on
the ownership or control of a wide range of personal property, including stocks
and other financial assets, business interests, art, intellectual property, retirement
accounts, and other savings and assets.
• Prop 42 would limit certain retroactive state taxes. This includes new taxes
based on conduct, activity, or status that occurred before the tax took effect.
• The restrictions would be difficult to change. Because they would be in the
Constitution, changing them in the future would require another vote of the
people. A tax that does not make sense today may be appropriate under different
circumstances in the future.
Prop 42 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both
Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 42 pass and Prop 42 receives more “yes”
votes, courts could find that the measures conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming
law. A court challenge could delay a final determination.

Election Countdown
11 days until the November election
We’ve gone over a lot of ballot props. That includes:
The wealth tax, or Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), and its countermeasures (https://voiceofsandiego.org/2026/10/09/how-to-make-sense-of-the-major-tax-propositions-on-the-ballot/), Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) and Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/)
Prop. 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), the initiative to change how California recalls officials (https://voiceofsandiego.org/2026/10/16/should-california-change-how-it-does-recall-elections/) and
Another proposal, Prop. 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/), to lift a ban that prohibits political candidates from financing their campaigns with public dollars.
This week, we’ll break down three bond measures on the ballot, which, if voters approve, would add a collective $45 billion before interest to the state’s debt for biomedical research, housing construction and home loans.
What to Know About Prop. 38
University budgets were rocked last year after the Trump administration slashed hundreds of federal research grants.
While much of that funding has been restored, the uncertainty left institutions cautious and looking to find alternative ways to fund research. An $8.4 billion bond to subsidize immunotherapy research to fight cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease could help address this, say backers of Prop. 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/).

Half of the money would go to a single University of California-affiliated institute, while the remaining $4.2 billion would be doled out to other select nonprofit and research organizations.
Any medications developed from research supported by the bond funding would have to be sold at a 20 percent discount to Californians and 10 percent of any revenue would go back to the state’s coffers.
Surgeon and billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson put it on the ballot. Medical groups such as the American Association of Immunologists are supporters, and Alzheimer’s San Diego said it is backing Prop. 38 because it’d more quickly provide treatment research to the nearly 100,000 people in the county living with Alzheimer’s or dementia. San Diego County Democrats also endorsed the measure.
The League of Women Voters and Stanford researcher and former National Institute of Health Director Robert Kaplan oppose it, arguing that billions of dollars for years to come shouldn’t just be for one field of health research.
Critics have also increasingly questioned why a single nonprofit would receive half the bond money. CalMatters’ reporting (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) showed that Michelson’s own institute, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, would be the beneficiary.
Michelson is Prop. 38’s primary financier, contributing $61 million of the Yes campaign’s $66 million total. Opponents have raised $9,000.
What to Know About Prop. 1 and Prop. 37, the Other Megabonds
The end is near in our bond measure journey. Here’s the quick and dirty run-down:
Voting yes on Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) would mean California could borrow $11.25 billion for all kinds of affordable housing programs, from rentals to student dormitories, to veteran and farmworker housing.
Democrats in the Legislature put this one on the ballot, and it’s backed by the governor and statewide apartment association who say it’ll spur much-needed building to address California’s homelessness and affordability crisis.
Some Republicans, including San Diego GOP Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), are not feeling it. He and others argue it would do little to make housing more affordable while taxpayers will be left on the hook.
Its cousin, Prop. 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), would create a loan program to allow private lenders to give up to 17 percent of the cost of a newly built home to would-be buyers. It’d do this by allowing the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in bonds.
A coalition of real estate and labor groups put the measure on the ballot, and SEIU and the California Association of Realtors are its bankrollers. They argue that in a state where the median home price is $900,000 (https://carorg.sharepoint.com/:x:/s/CAR-RE-PublicProducts/IQAK-pU7cef4QpkWsCPlxwZKAbdKLa3OO0vFwHpuH_FADK8?rtime=7Fo4fkkx30g), it’d create a pathway for middle-class families to enter into homeownership.
But … but … but …
Doesn’t that mean taking on even more debt?
Yes, critics such as the League of Women Voters say. They think it’s not a good idea to let people buy homes they otherwise can’t afford by allowing buyers to go deeper into debt.
Unconventional Alliances
Things get curious if we zoom-in on Prop.38’s backers and naysayers.
Take the California Democratic Party, to which Michelson is a longtime donor. The Los Angeles-based philanthropist physician has given more than $100,000 to Democrats this cycle alone. That includes at least $25,0000 to Xavier Becerra in his campaign for governor as well as nearly $80,000 to fellow Angeleno Antonio Villaraigosa for his failed gubernatorial bid. He’s also donated to Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/robert-rivas-165041)’ re-election campaign.
Michelson has spread his fortune in San Diego, too. In 2020, he gave Assemblymember Tasha Boerner (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tasha-boerner-horvath-165421) $4,700 for her re-election campaign, and labor leader and former Assemblymember Lorena Gonzalez received thousands of dollars from Michelson for her 2020 re-election campaign. Two years later, he gave more than $10,000 to her brief, unsuccessful run for secretary of state.
The California GOP has endorsed Prop. 38, while choosing to stay neutral on Prop. 1, the $11 billion bond to build more affordable housing, and Prop. 37, the $25 billion bond to help finance new homeowners’ mortgages. DeMaio also supports the immunology research bond, saying in a podcast episode (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/videos/ca-voter-guide-yes-to-prop-38-no-on-prop-44) that it’s a better deal for taxpayers than to most other loans because therapies developed with the funding would be sold at a discount to consumers. He is against the two housing bonds.
Meanwhile, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association opposes all three bond measures, which they call an inappropriate use of public funds. They argue that biomedical research should be financed by pharmaceutical companies or the federal government rather than California residents.
They’re in company with the League of Women Voters who similarly argue that Prop. 38 is a misappropriation of public dollars, and that such funding shouldn’t be directed toward one UC-affiliated nonprofit.
Plenty of state lawmakers from the San Diego area didn’t want to wade in on this one, though, with one notable exception.
In a statement, San Diego Assemblymember Chris Ward (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/christopher-ward-35497) said he’s against the research bond because the funding would go to the one institution rather than to other California researchers who are best positioned to find cures and deliver treatments. He supports the housing bonds.
Getting responses from other Democrats, meanwhile, proved difficult.
Derek Humphrey, a campaign spokesperson for Boerner, said she doesn’t take public positions on propositions because she believes voters should weigh in on them, not their elected officials.
Chula Vista Assemblymember David Alvarez (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/david-alvarez-112993) is still undecided about the research bond, campaign manager Chris Jonsmyr said, but he supports both of the housing measures.
Campaign manager Skyler Johnson did not respond to emails asking if Encinitas state Sen. Catherine Blakespear supports or opposes Prop. 38, nor did Jeremy Addis-Mills, campaign manager for state Sen. Akilah Weber Pierson .
