PROP 1 VETERANS & AFFORDABLE HOUSING BONDS SUPPORT
Funding from the 2018 bond for broad affordable housing programs has been spent, and
there is a corresponding backlog of affordable housing projects stuck waiting for years
for financing. Many families in California continue to endure high housing costs, leading
to an increase in homelessness and overcrowding. Public subsidy is necessary to provide
safe and stable housing for households at the lowest incomes.
Prop 1 authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds for the construction,
acquisition, rehabilitation, and preservation of affordable housing and for
homeownership programs, plus $1.25 billion, also in general obligation bonds, for
veteran mortgage assistance through the CalVet Home Loan Program, expected to be
repaid from borrowers’ mortgage payments.
Vote YES on Proposition 1
PROP 2 SAVE FOR CALIFORNIA’S FUTURE ACT SUPPORT
Proposition 2 will allow California to save more money during strong economic years so
it can protect schools and other essential services when revenues fall.
California’s budget can change dramatically from one year to the next. The state relies
heavily on personal income taxes, including taxes on capital gains. Capital gains are
profits people earn when they sell stocks, businesses, real estate, or other investments.
These taxes bring in much more money when financial markets are doing well, but that
revenue can disappear quickly during an economic downturn.
Prop 2 would help California prepare for those swings. It would allow the state to build a
larger rainy-day fund and require it to save more when capital gains revenues are
2
unusually high. That would give California a stronger financial cushion during recessions,
natural disasters, public health emergencies, and other difficult periods.
Saving more during good years can help prevent deep cuts to public services during bad
years. It can also reduce the need for emergency borrowing and other painful budget
actions.
Vote YES on Proposition 2
PROP 3 CHILDREN'S EDUCATION & HEALTH CARE PROTECTION SUPPORT
Proposition 3 would protect funding for schools, health care, and other essential services
by keeping California’s current income tax rates on the highest-income 2 percent of
taxpayers. Without Prop 3, those rates would fall in 2031, reducing state revenue by an
estimated $5 billion to $15 billion each year. Prop 3 would not change anyone’s tax rate
today.
About 40 percent of this revenue goes to schools and community colleges. The rest
helps fund Medi-Cal and other health and human services, other essential public
services, and state budget reserves.
California should not give its highest-income residents a multi-billion-dollar tax cut while
schools, health care, and other essential services face serious financial pressure. Prop 3
simply asks the top 2 percent to keep paying the same rates they already pay. The
League strongly supports the measure because it protects vital services, helps California
weather economic downturns, and keeps the state’s tax system fair.
Vote YES on Proposition 3
PROP 4 CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT SUPPORT
Elections should be won, not bought. But in California, personal wealth and access to big
donors have become unofficial qualifications for public office. Qualified candidates
without wealthy networks are often shut out before voters hear their ideas, while
candidates and officeholders spend too much time chasing large checks.
Prop 4 gives Californians a way to change that. It lifts California’s near-total ban on
public campaign financing and allows the state and local governments to create
voluntary programs. The measure creates no financing program and provides no
campaign funding by itself. Each jurisdiction decides whether to adopt a program and
how to design and pay for it.
3
Public financing can make small donations matter more, give candidates without
personal fortunes a fairer chance to compete, and let them spend more time listening to
voters. By reducing the advantage of incumbents, wealthy donors, and special interests,
these programs can make elections more open, competitive, and accountable.
They can also open the door to candidates who better reflect California. Latino, Asian
American or Pacific Islander, and Black Californians make up nearly two-thirds of our
population but remain vastly underrepresented in local government across much of the
state. High campaign costs help keep that barrier in place. When voters can choose
candidates who understand their communities and reflect their interests, they have more
reason to participate.
Prop 4 protects public money. Candidates must show broad grassroots support and
agree to spending limits. Money reserved for education, transportation, or public safety
cannot be used. Programs cannot favor incumbents or discriminate by party. Public
funds cannot pay legal defense costs or fines or repay a candidate’s personal loan to a
campaign. Finally, the measure triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign money in
California elections.
Prop 4 gives every California community the freedom to build elections where voters
have more power and wealthy donors and special interests have less.
Vote YES on Proposition 4
(The LWVC is an official proponent and has signed ballot arguments.)
PROP 5 RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS SUPPORT
California's recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official. It should never
become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a
small fraction of voters. However, that is exactly what today's recall rules allow, since the
same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets
the most votes, even if that's far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process. Voters are asked to remove an
officer by majority vote, then hand that same office to a replacement chosen by
whomever gets the most votes, often in a field crowded with dozens of candidates and
with no requirement that the winner reach half the vote. That’s a loophole that can
easily be exploited. In 2021, had the recall against Governor Newsom succeeded, the
leading replacement candidate would have taken office with the support of just 28% of
recall voters, a stark illustration of exactly this problem.
4
Prop 5 restores the recall to its proper purpose: deciding whether an official should
remain in office. It shuts down that back door with one clean fix: removing the
replacement candidate vote from the recall ballot itself. If a recall succeeds, the vacancy
is filled through succession, appointment, or a later election decided by real majority
support. These are the same rules used to fill any other vacancy in state government. A
recalled officer can still run again later. This is a pro-democracy safeguard too - the
choice stays with voters rather than being taken away entirely. What Prop 5 rules out is
any return to office through appointment, so a recalled officer can only reclaim the seat
by winning a real vote.
This is a matter of basic fairness and majority rule. Prop 5 protects accountability while
ending a system that can hand power to a candidate most voters never chose.
Vote YES on Proposition 5
(The LWVC is an official proponent and has signed ballot arguments.)
PROP 37 LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OPPOSE
OF NEW HOMES
California must build more homes and make homeownership possible for more families.
The League of Women Voters of California has worked toward those goals for decades
and supports Prop 1, which would provide $10 billion for affordable housing and
homeownership programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans.
Prop 37 addresses a real barrier: the down payment. But it does so by adding a second
mortgage that buyers generally would repay every month.
• Prop 37 could help a family buy a home without making it affordable to keep.
Buyers generally would repay the Prop 37 loan each month in addition to their
first mortgage, property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other costs. Voters would
not know the interest rate, loan term, or monthly payment before approving the
program.
• The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting
families facing the greatest barriers. Generations of housing discrimination have
left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives
no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or
former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income
could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers
would still have to provide at least 3 percent of the home price.
• The program is not tied to good planning. Assistance could be used only for
5
newly built or newly converted homes, with no requirement that they be near
jobs, transit, schools, or services or avoid areas with high transportation,
insurance, or natural-hazard costs.
• Too much remains undecided. The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether
investors would buy the bonds, how the loans would compare in cost with other
assistance, or whether the program would result in more homes being built or
purchased. The interest rate and repayment terms would be set after the election.
California needs homeownership programs that lower families’ total costs, confront
racial barriers to building wealth, and support strong communities. Prop 37 does not
meet that test.
Vote NO on Proposition 37
PROP 38 BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH OPPOSE
Medical research can save lives, but Prop 38 is the wrong way to fund it. It would
authorize $8.4 billion in borrowing for immunology and immunotherapy research and
require the state to make $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for
about 20 years. Those payments would come from the General Fund, which also pays
for schools, health care, and other public services.
• Borrowing is a poor way to pay for ongoing scientific research. Bonds are best
suited to long-lived investments such as buildings and infrastructure. With
interest, the Legislative Analyst estimates Prop 38 would cost about 10 percent
more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the research up front.
• Prop 38 would lock billions of dollars into one field of research for years to
come. About half of the money would go to a single UC-affiliated research
institute and the other half to a grant program, with at least $4.2 billion reserved
for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research. Scientific opportunities and
public health needs change. State funding should be able to respond to those
changes rather than locking billions of dollars into one field of research through a
ballot measure.
• Research royalties are no reason to take on $8.4 billion in debt. When voters
approved $3 billion for stem-cell research in 2004, supporters pointed to royalties
and millions in new state revenue. By 2022, CIRM reported only $15.6 million in
its licensing and royalties fund from royalty payments. Prop 38 again points to
research-generated revenue as a way to offset public costs, but the Legislative
Analyst says the amount and timing are unknown.
6
California can support important medical research without committing taxpayers to
decades of debt and restricting future choices about where limited public dollars can do
the most good.
Vote NO on Proposition 38
PROP 39 PROHIBITS VOTING WITHOUT OPPOSE
GOVERNMENT-ISSUED ID
Prop 39 is a partisan power grab to further President Trump’s voter suppression efforts.
It is based on lies about our elections. Prop 39 is intended to make it harder to vote and
easier for politicians to decide which voters count. Right-wing billionaires spent millions
to put it on the ballot.
• California's elections are already secure. Voters swear to citizenship under
penalty of perjury, and officials verify identity at registration, check the rolls in
person, and match every mail ballot signature.
• A new registration hurdle. Millions of existing voters could be forced to
effectively re-register to “designate” a government ID for mail voting, like a
driver's license or Social Security number.
• Identity theft risk. You would be required to put the last four digits of that
sensitive ID number on the outside of your ballot envelope – next to your name,
address, and signature.
• Valid ballots thrown out. Your mailed ballot would not be counted if the number
you wrote didn’t match the “designated” number. One wrong digit or a blank field
could sink a valid ballot, with no guaranteed notice or chance to fix it. Texas tried
this and rejected one in eight mail ballots. Those voters were less likely to vote
again.
• An ID check every time you vote in person. You would have to show a
government-issued ID every time, even after officials verified who you are. Most
voters turned away under similar laws elsewhere had qualifying ID, just not on
them.
• A modern-day poll tax. A “free” ID is not free. Getting one costs transportation,
childcare, time off work, and fees for the paperwork behind it. Seniors, students,
low-income workers, voters with disabilities, and voters of color are hit hardest.
• Valid ID still must match. Nearly 30 percent of U.S. adults have changed their
name, 94 percent of them women. Californians who took a new name at marriage,
and transgender voters whose documents lag may hold valid ID and be turned
away anyway.
7
• Bad data and wrongful purges. Citizenship checks would likely run through
untrustworthy federal databases that wrongly flag eligible citizens to purge them
from voter rolls.
• Longer lines and slower results. Extra ID checks and flagged ballots add delay,
and the lawsuits would stretch it further, handing election deniers more time to
spread lies.
• Hundreds of millions of dollars every year. New systems, staffing, free ID cards,
audits, and lawsuits, all paid for while California already has budget problems.
Don't let President Trump and right-wing billionaires decide whose vote counts.
Vote NO on Proposition 39
(The LWVC is an official opponent and has signed ballot arguments.)
PROP 40 BILLIONAIRE TAX NEUTRAL
Prop 40 would tax extreme wealth to help meet urgent needs, but its one-time structure
conflicts with principles of sound public finance and risks long-term revenue loss.
The federal government is walking away from feeding people and providing access to
basic health care, putting Medi-Cal coverage and CalFresh benefits at risk for millions of
Californians. When it does, the state has a responsibility to step in. Prop 40 would
impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on billionaire wealth. The state would direct 90% of
the revenue to health care, with the remaining 10% going to education, food assistance,
and administration of the wealth tax. That could deliver tens of billions to the safety net
when families are losing both.
The measure also confronts a deeper problem the League cannot ignore. The wealthiest
American households pay a lower total effective tax rate than the whole population,
largely because business wealth produces little taxable income. As of September 2025,
roughly 900 American billionaires held nearly double the wealth of the entire bottom
half of the country. Inequality on that scale demands that solutions like wealth taxes get
serious consideration.
On the con side, Prop 40 makes budget decisions at the ballot box, locking the proceeds
into an earmarked fund. The Legislature could choose how to spend within those
categories but could not redirect the money to other needs. A one-time tax is also only a
stopgap for programs that need funding every year. Furthermore, the tax rests on only a
few hundred people. Of these, six billionaires reportedly left the state before the January
1, 2026, cutoff, potentially erasing more than one-quarter of the proponents’ projected
8
$100 billion revenue. It should be noted that the government estimates only tens of
billions of dollars raised over several years and says the amount is highly uncertain. The
government also estimates that state revenue could be reduced by less than $1 billion
per year.
The deeper fear is behavioral: that the tax pushes billionaires out after they pay and
deters others from ever coming. The government offers only the broad estimate that
state revenue could be reduced by below $1 billion per year. On the other hand, some
research finds that tax-driven migration among the wealthy is modest, and Silicon
Valley's ecosystem is not easily traded away.
The human need is urgent and asking those most able to pay to fill a hole the federal
government created is a fair demand. But the tax mechanism limits legislative flexibility
for allocating money where it is most crucial and raises the risk of taxpayer flight.
Because we have strong positions on both sides of this measure, the League takes a
neutral position on Prop 40.
PROP 41 LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES & REQUIRES SPECIAL TAX AUDITS OPPOSE
Prop 41 would put revenue from new state taxes under the Gann Limit’s rigid
constitutional spending cap, making it harder to fund essential services and respond to
changing needs. It would apply to any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after
January 1, 2026.
The League opposed the Gann Initiative in 1979 because its spending limit was too
inflexible to assure adequate government services in an uncertain future. Prop 41 would
extend that constraint to new tax revenue. This is especially concerning for voter-
approved initiatives, which generally cannot be changed by the Legislature without
another vote of the people.
Prop 41 would also require audits of programs funded by new or increased special taxes,
including programs such as public campaign financing that may not receive General Fund
support. If a new tax excluded its revenue from the Gann Limit, the state could not
impose, collect, or enforce it. And when the state is at or near the limit, Prop 41 could
prevent all the revenue voters approved for a specific purpose from being spent on that
purpose.
The audits would add state costs, estimated by the Legislative Analyst’s Office in the low
millions of dollars annually and growing over time. The General Fund would pay for a
9
pre-election audit if an initiative failed to qualify or is rejected by voters. New programs
could also be difficult to evaluate before they exist.
Prop 41 is also designed to prevail over a conflicting initiative on the same ballot. If both
Prop 40, the Billionaire Tax measure, and Prop 41 pass and Prop 41 receives more “yes”
votes, courts could find that they conflict and prevent Prop 40 from becoming law.
Litigation could delay a final determination.
Vote NO on Proposition 41
PROP 42 LIMITS NEW STATE TAXES ON PERSONAL PROPERTY OPPOSE
Prop 42 would lock broad new restrictions on state taxing power into the California
Constitution, limiting California’s ability to respond to future needs.

the ownership or control of a wide range of personal property, including stocks
and other financial assets, business interests, art, intellectual property, retirement
accounts, and other savings and assets.
• Prop 42 would limit certain retroactive state taxes. This includes new taxes
based on conduct, activity, or status that occurred before the tax took effect.
• The restrictions would be difficult to change. Because they would be in the
Constitution, changing them in the future would require another vote of the
people. A tax that does not make sense today may be appropriate under different
circumstances in the future.

On the ballot this November, Californians will decide if they want the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support research that aims to deliver cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease “in our lifetime.”
Backers say (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) that Proposition 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases and provide a steady funding source amid uncertainty of federal grants. The measure ensures “strong accountability, including independent audits,” and mandates a 20% discount to California residents for treatments developed from this funding.
But critics view the legislation as a Trojan horse: while promising transformative medical breakthroughs, it will channel billions in state funding to a newly created institute that currently has no scientists or researchers.
If Proposition 38 passes, San Diego stands to be a major beneficiary.
The La Jolla Institute for Immunology, Salk Institute, Sanford Burnham Prebys, UC San Diego and Scripps Research — some of the most prominent immunology research institutions in the nation — would likely be on an advisory committee overseeing $4.2 billion, about half of the bond revenue the proposition would generate.
Despite their potential financial stake in its passage, each organization has declined to speak about the measure.
What Proposition 38 says
A “yes” vote would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research for diseases like cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease.
The funding will primarily target early-stage research. In theory, intellectual property developed from this research could be licensed to pharmaceutical companies and biotechnology companies to turn discoveries into drugs.
Under the licensing terms, institutes agree to a 5% to 10% royalty on intellectual property developed. About 10% of all resulting revenue will go toward repaying the state bond. Once the bond is fully repaid, 100% of the revenue will return to research.
The proposition ensures that no more than 2% of all money dispersed goes to administrative expenses, keeping the bulk of state funds focused on research. However, a special carve-out provides the chosen institution additional flexibility, offering a $100 million loan for “startup costs.”
The lion’s share of the funding will be overseen by a single nonprofit research institution that is not named in the measure.
“The intent of the measure is to create in the institute a ‘hub’ of sorts for immunology and immunotherapy research, which will bring together scientists … to accelerate discoveries into treatments and cures,” said Robin Swanson, spokeswoman from Yes on Prop 38.
One institute will get half the funds
Half of the $8.4 billion is earmarked for a single institution — unnamed in Proposition 38.
The measure calls for the California Department of Public Health to select “a world-class and innovative immunology and immunotherapy research institute affiliated with the University of California.”
The recipient must meet a set of highly specific criteria, and according to CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), only one institution satisfies this threshold: the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
When asked to confirm, Proposition 38 spokeswoman Swanson acknowledged it is “very likely” CIII will be chosen.
CIII is (https://www.calimmunology.org/)a UCLA-affiliated nonprofit founded in 2024 by Dr. Gary Michelson, Meyer Luskin, Michael Milken, Sean Parker and other biotech billionaires.
Notably, the proposition’s primary future beneficiaries are funding the campaign.
Campaign finance records show that of the more than $38 million raised by the “Yes on 38” campaign, the vast majority has come from Michelson and Luskin, including a $14 million loan from Michelson to his own nonprofit organization supporting the measure.

Proposition 38 was written in a way that ensures more than $4 billion in borrowed state funds would go to an institution affiliated with UCLA. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 23, 2026 at 2:10 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Proposition 38 sounds constructive. It proposes allowing the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund advanced biomedical research into cures for heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other illnesses. But its key provisions show the measure is something much different: another effort by deep-pocketed individuals and organizations to use the California initiative process for their own benefit.
This was hammered home by a CalMatters analysis (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that found the measure’s fine print was written in a way to ensure that $4 billion-plus of the borrowed funds would go to “one institute in the entire state: the [UCLA-affiliated] California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.” This was done by requiring the funds be given to a nonprofit research organization founded before 2025 that focuses on immunology and immunotherapy and that is affiliated with a UC campus with a medical center (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026) that has “greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year,” per the (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) California Secretary of State’s Office. This crucial fact isn’t mentioned in Proposition 38’s ballot language or its campaign literature.
Now here’s where the initiative’s shadiness becomes obvious: A spokesperson for the measure insists that the oddly specific criteria weren’t intended to direct billions to any institution in particular. Yeah, sure. It’s just a mammoth coincidence, you see, that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy was co-founded by Gary K. Michelson, one of the two billionaires who are the chief backers of Proposition 38.
A prominent scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine has emerged as the measure’s most persuasive critic. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federal National Institutes of Health, which has been the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research since the late 1940s (https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/spotlight/tl/feature/nih). He believes it’s impossible to justify giving so much funding to one institution, given how much promising immunology and immunotherapy research is underway in California.
If the measure passes, an LAO analysis says it will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years to pay off. To address concerns about the cost to a state facing years of structural deficits, proponents assert it’s a real possibility that the principal and interest on the borrowed $8.4 billion could be repaid to the state because of the Proposition 38 provision that 10% of revenue generated by discoveries funded by the measure must go directly to the general fund of the state budget. But Kaplan notes that similar claims were made in 2004 when state voters authorized $3 billion in bonds for stem-cell research. To date, the state has only received about $16 million in royalties.
Proposition 38 is an $8.4 billion wolf in sheep’s clothing. The Union-Tribune Editorial Board urges voters to take a stand for honesty, transparency and fiscal sanity by opposing it.

On the ballot this November, Californians will decide if they want the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support research that aims to deliver cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease “in our lifetime.”
Backers say (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) that Proposition 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases and provide a steady funding source amid uncertainty of federal grants. The measure ensures “strong accountability, including independent audits,” and mandates a 20% discount to California residents for treatments developed from this funding.
But critics view the legislation as a Trojan horse: while promising transformative medical breakthroughs, it will channel billions in state funding to a newly created institute that currently has no scientists or researchers.
If Proposition 38 passes, San Diego stands to be a major beneficiary.
The La Jolla Institute for Immunology, Salk Institute, Sanford Burnham Prebys, UC San Diego and Scripps Research — some of the most prominent immunology research institutions in the nation — would likely be on an advisory committee overseeing $4.2 billion, about half of the bond revenue the proposition would generate.
Despite their potential financial stake in its passage, each organization has declined to speak about the measure.
What Proposition 38 says
A “yes” vote would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research for diseases like cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease.
The funding will primarily target early-stage research. In theory, intellectual property developed from this research could be licensed to pharmaceutical companies and biotechnology companies to turn discoveries into drugs.
Under the licensing terms, institutes agree to a 5% to 10% royalty on intellectual property developed. About 10% of all resulting revenue will go toward repaying the state bond. Once the bond is fully repaid, 100% of the revenue will return to research.
The proposition ensures that no more than 2% of all money dispersed goes to administrative expenses, keeping the bulk of state funds focused on research. However, a special carve-out provides the chosen institution additional flexibility, offering a $100 million loan for “startup costs.”
The lion’s share of the funding will be overseen by a single nonprofit research institution that is not named in the measure.
“The intent of the measure is to create in the institute a ‘hub’ of sorts for immunology and immunotherapy research, which will bring together scientists … to accelerate discoveries into treatments and cures,” said Robin Swanson, spokeswoman from Yes on Prop 38.
One institute will get half the funds
Half of the $8.4 billion is earmarked for a single institution — unnamed in Proposition 38.
The measure calls for the California Department of Public Health to select “a world-class and innovative immunology and immunotherapy research institute affiliated with the University of California.”
The recipient must meet a set of highly specific criteria, and according to CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), only one institution satisfies this threshold: the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
When asked to confirm, Proposition 38 spokeswoman Swanson acknowledged it is “very likely” CIII will be chosen.
CIII is (https://www.calimmunology.org/)a UCLA-affiliated nonprofit founded in 2024 by Dr. Gary Michelson, Meyer Luskin, Michael Milken, Sean Parker and other biotech billionaires.
Notably, the proposition’s primary future beneficiaries are funding the campaign.
Campaign finance records show that of the more than $38 million raised by the “Yes on 38” campaign, the vast majority has come from Michelson and Luskin, including a $14 million loan from Michelson to his own nonprofit organization supporting the measure.

On the ballot this November, Californians will decide if they want the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support research that aims to deliver cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease “in our lifetime.”
Backers say (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) that Proposition 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases and provide a steady funding source amid uncertainty of federal grants. The measure ensures “strong accountability, including independent audits,” and mandates a 20% discount to California residents for treatments developed from this funding.
But critics view the legislation as a Trojan horse: while promising transformative medical breakthroughs, it will channel billions in state funding to a newly created institute that currently has no scientists or researchers.
If Proposition 38 passes, San Diego stands to be a major beneficiary.
The La Jolla Institute for Immunology, Salk Institute, Sanford Burnham Prebys, UC San Diego and Scripps Research — some of the most prominent immunology research institutions in the nation — would likely be on an advisory committee overseeing $4.2 billion, about half of the bond revenue the proposition would generate.
Despite their potential financial stake in its passage, each organization has declined to speak about the measure.
What Proposition 38 says
A “yes” vote would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research for diseases like cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease.
The funding will primarily target early-stage research. In theory, intellectual property developed from this research could be licensed to pharmaceutical companies and biotechnology companies to turn discoveries into drugs.
Under the licensing terms, institutes agree to a 5% to 10% royalty on intellectual property developed. About 10% of all resulting revenue will go toward repaying the state bond. Once the bond is fully repaid, 100% of the revenue will return to research.
The proposition ensures that no more than 2% of all money dispersed goes to administrative expenses, keeping the bulk of state funds focused on research. However, a special carve-out provides the chosen institution additional flexibility, offering a $100 million loan for “startup costs.”
The lion’s share of the funding will be overseen by a single nonprofit research institution that is not named in the measure.
“The intent of the measure is to create in the institute a ‘hub’ of sorts for immunology and immunotherapy research, which will bring together scientists … to accelerate discoveries into treatments and cures,” said Robin Swanson, spokeswoman from Yes on Prop 38.
One institute will get half the funds
Half of the $8.4 billion is earmarked for a single institution — unnamed in Proposition 38.
The measure calls for the California Department of Public Health to select “a world-class and innovative immunology and immunotherapy research institute affiliated with the University of California.”
The recipient must meet a set of highly specific criteria, and according to CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), only one institution satisfies this threshold: the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
When asked to confirm, Proposition 38 spokeswoman Swanson acknowledged it is “very likely” CIII will be chosen.
CIII is (https://www.calimmunology.org/)a UCLA-affiliated nonprofit founded in 2024 by Dr. Gary Michelson, Meyer Luskin, Michael Milken, Sean Parker and other biotech billionaires.
Notably, the proposition’s primary future beneficiaries are funding the campaign.
Campaign finance records show that of the more than $38 million raised by the “Yes on 38” campaign, the vast majority has come from Michelson and Luskin, including a $14 million loan from Michelson to his own nonprofit organization supporting the measure.

Proposition 38 was written in a way that ensures more than $4 billion in borrowed state funds would go to an institution affiliated with UCLA. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 23, 2026 at 2:10 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Proposition 38 sounds constructive. It proposes allowing the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund advanced biomedical research into cures for heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other illnesses. But its key provisions show the measure is something much different: another effort by deep-pocketed individuals and organizations to use the California initiative process for their own benefit.
This was hammered home by a CalMatters analysis (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that found the measure’s fine print was written in a way to ensure that $4 billion-plus of the borrowed funds would go to “one institute in the entire state: the [UCLA-affiliated] California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.” This was done by requiring the funds be given to a nonprofit research organization founded before 2025 that focuses on immunology and immunotherapy and that is affiliated with a UC campus with a medical center (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026) that has “greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year,” per the (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) California Secretary of State’s Office. This crucial fact isn’t mentioned in Proposition 38’s ballot language or its campaign literature.
Now here’s where the initiative’s shadiness becomes obvious: A spokesperson for the measure insists that the oddly specific criteria weren’t intended to direct billions to any institution in particular. Yeah, sure. It’s just a mammoth coincidence, you see, that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy was co-founded by Gary K. Michelson, one of the two billionaires who are the chief backers of Proposition 38.
A prominent scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine has emerged as the measure’s most persuasive critic. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federal National Institutes of Health, which has been the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research since the late 1940s (https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/spotlight/tl/feature/nih). He believes it’s impossible to justify giving so much funding to one institution, given how much promising immunology and immunotherapy research is underway in California.
If the measure passes, an LAO analysis says it will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years to pay off. To address concerns about the cost to a state facing years of structural deficits, proponents assert it’s a real possibility that the principal and interest on the borrowed $8.4 billion could be repaid to the state because of the Proposition 38 provision that 10% of revenue generated by discoveries funded by the measure must go directly to the general fund of the state budget. But Kaplan notes that similar claims were made in 2004 when state voters authorized $3 billion in bonds for stem-cell research. To date, the state has only received about $16 million in royalties.
Proposition 38 is an $8.4 billion wolf in sheep’s clothing. The Union-Tribune Editorial Board urges voters to take a stand for honesty, transparency and fiscal sanity by opposing it.

Proposition 38 was written in a way that ensures more than $4 billion in borrowed state funds would go to an institution affiliated with UCLA. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 23, 2026 at 2:10 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Proposition 38 sounds constructive. It proposes allowing the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund advanced biomedical research into cures for heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other illnesses. But its key provisions show the measure is something much different: another effort by deep-pocketed individuals and organizations to use the California initiative process for their own benefit.
This was hammered home by a CalMatters analysis (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that found the measure’s fine print was written in a way to ensure that $4 billion-plus of the borrowed funds would go to “one institute in the entire state: the [UCLA-affiliated] California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.” This was done by requiring the funds be given to a nonprofit research organization founded before 2025 that focuses on immunology and immunotherapy and that is affiliated with a UC campus with a medical center (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026) that has “greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year,” per the (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) California Secretary of State’s Office. This crucial fact isn’t mentioned in Proposition 38’s ballot language or its campaign literature.
Now here’s where the initiative’s shadiness becomes obvious: A spokesperson for the measure insists that the oddly specific criteria weren’t intended to direct billions to any institution in particular. Yeah, sure. It’s just a mammoth coincidence, you see, that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy was co-founded by Gary K. Michelson, one of the two billionaires who are the chief backers of Proposition 38.
A prominent scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine has emerged as the measure’s most persuasive critic. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federal National Institutes of Health, which has been the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research since the late 1940s (https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/spotlight/tl/feature/nih). He believes it’s impossible to justify giving so much funding to one institution, given how much promising immunology and immunotherapy research is underway in California.
If the measure passes, an LAO analysis says it will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years to pay off. To address concerns about the cost to a state facing years of structural deficits, proponents assert it’s a real possibility that the principal and interest on the borrowed $8.4 billion could be repaid to the state because of the Proposition 38 provision that 10% of revenue generated by discoveries funded by the measure must go directly to the general fund of the state budget. But Kaplan notes that similar claims were made in 2004 when state voters authorized $3 billion in bonds for stem-cell research. To date, the state has only received about $16 million in royalties.
Proposition 38 is an $8.4 billion wolf in sheep’s clothing. The Union-Tribune Editorial Board urges voters to take a stand for honesty, transparency and fiscal sanity by opposing it.

By Noelle Harff (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/noelle-harff/) | noelle.harff@sduniontribune.com (mailto:noelle.harff@sduniontribune.com)
PUBLISHED: October 2, 2026 at 1:36 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 3, 2026 at 4:24 PM PDT

On the ballot this November, Californians will decide if they want the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support research that aims to deliver cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease “in our lifetime.”
Backers say (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm) that Proposition 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases and provide a steady funding source amid uncertainty of federal grants. The measure ensures “strong accountability, including independent audits,” and mandates a 20% discount to California residents for treatments developed from this funding.
But critics view the legislation as a Trojan horse: while promising transformative medical breakthroughs, it will channel billions in state funding to a newly created institute that currently has no scientists or researchers.
If Proposition 38 passes, San Diego stands to be a major beneficiary.
The La Jolla Institute for Immunology, Salk Institute, Sanford Burnham Prebys, UC San Diego and Scripps Research — some of the most prominent immunology research institutions in the nation — would likely be on an advisory committee overseeing $4.2 billion, about half of the bond revenue the proposition would generate.
Despite their potential financial stake in its passage, each organization has declined to speak about the measure.
What Proposition 38 says
A “yes” vote would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research for diseases like cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease.
The funding will primarily target early-stage research. In theory, intellectual property developed from this research could be licensed to pharmaceutical companies and biotechnology companies to turn discoveries into drugs.
Under the licensing terms, institutes agree to a 5% to 10% royalty on intellectual property developed. About 10% of all resulting revenue will go toward repaying the state bond. Once the bond is fully repaid, 100% of the revenue will return to research.
The proposition ensures that no more than 2% of all money dispersed goes to administrative expenses, keeping the bulk of state funds focused on research. However, a special carve-out provides the chosen institution additional flexibility, offering a $100 million loan for “startup costs.”
The lion’s share of the funding will be overseen by a single nonprofit research institution that is not named in the measure.
“The intent of the measure is to create in the institute a ‘hub’ of sorts for immunology and immunotherapy research, which will bring together scientists … to accelerate discoveries into treatments and cures,” said Robin Swanson, spokeswoman from Yes on Prop 38.
One institute will get half the funds
Half of the $8.4 billion is earmarked for a single institution — unnamed in Proposition 38.
The measure calls for the California Department of Public Health to select “a world-class and innovative immunology and immunotherapy research institute affiliated with the University of California.”
The recipient must meet a set of highly specific criteria, and according to CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), only one institution satisfies this threshold: the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy (CIII).
When asked to confirm, Proposition 38 spokeswoman Swanson acknowledged it is “very likely” CIII will be chosen.
CIII is (https://www.calimmunology.org/)a UCLA-affiliated nonprofit founded in 2024 by Dr. Gary Michelson, Meyer Luskin, Michael Milken, Sean Parker and other biotech billionaires.
Notably, the proposition’s primary future beneficiaries are funding the campaign.
Campaign finance records show that of the more than $38 million raised by the “Yes on 38” campaign, the vast majority has come from Michelson and Luskin, including a $14 million loan from Michelson to his own nonprofit organization supporting the measure.

Proposition 38 was written in a way that ensures more than $4 billion in borrowed state funds would go to an institution affiliated with UCLA. (SCNG)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 23, 2026 at 2:10 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Proposition 38 sounds constructive. It proposes allowing the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund advanced biomedical research into cures for heart disease, Alzheimer’s and other illnesses. But its key provisions show the measure is something much different: another effort by deep-pocketed individuals and organizations to use the California initiative process for their own benefit.
This was hammered home by a CalMatters analysis (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that found the measure’s fine print was written in a way to ensure that $4 billion-plus of the borrowed funds would go to “one institute in the entire state: the [UCLA-affiliated] California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.” This was done by requiring the funds be given to a nonprofit research organization founded before 2025 that focuses on immunology and immunotherapy and that is affiliated with a UC campus with a medical center (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026) that has “greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year,” per the (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) California Secretary of State’s Office. This crucial fact isn’t mentioned in Proposition 38’s ballot language or its campaign literature.
Now here’s where the initiative’s shadiness becomes obvious: A spokesperson for the measure insists that the oddly specific criteria weren’t intended to direct billions to any institution in particular. Yeah, sure. It’s just a mammoth coincidence, you see, that the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy was co-founded by Gary K. Michelson, one of the two billionaires who are the chief backers of Proposition 38.
A prominent scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine has emerged as the measure’s most persuasive critic. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federal National Institutes of Health, which has been the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research since the late 1940s (https://profiles.nlm.nih.gov/spotlight/tl/feature/nih). He believes it’s impossible to justify giving so much funding to one institution, given how much promising immunology and immunotherapy research is underway in California.
If the measure passes, an LAO analysis says it will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years to pay off. To address concerns about the cost to a state facing years of structural deficits, proponents assert it’s a real possibility that the principal and interest on the borrowed $8.4 billion could be repaid to the state because of the Proposition 38 provision that 10% of revenue generated by discoveries funded by the measure must go directly to the general fund of the state budget. But Kaplan notes that similar claims were made in 2004 when state voters authorized $3 billion in bonds for stem-cell research. To date, the state has only received about $16 million in royalties.
Proposition 38 is an $8.4 billion wolf in sheep’s clothing. The Union-Tribune Editorial Board urges voters to take a stand for honesty, transparency and fiscal sanity by opposing it.

I'm weighing the strongest argument for "yes" to be fair. Immunotherapy is a promising field, and $8.4B spread over roughly a decade would add about $840M a year, which is meaningful against NIH's overall budget and California's share of it.

Next I'm checking the federal funding angle: the Trump administration cut and froze grants, and although Congress restored most of the money, the uncertainty is still there. I'm also weighing whether the competitive grants half, which goes to UC campuses, Stanford, Caltech, Scripps, and others, could do real good even if the institute half is shaky. The cost is roughly $500 to 600 million a year, about a quarter of a percent of the general fund, and the endorsements from Newsom, both parties, patient groups, and immunologist and labor organizations point toward support.

Now I'm weighing the case against it: the measure would direct $4.2B to one unproven nonprofit tied to its main funder, with criteria that seem written around that single entity. The institute itself is barely operating so far, with only a handful of staff, no director, and an unfinished building.

The measure's design gives this nonprofit an unusual amount of power, including exemptions from the Public Records Act, open meetings law, and conflict-of-interest disclosure, along with a role in bond issuance, grant decisions, and licensing. Termination looks difficult too, and I'm checking how hard it would be to undo.

Now I'm going through the measure's remaining design problems: the grants council is made up of representatives from the same institutions that can receive grants, which creates self-dealing risk, and the Legislature can't amend the allocation provisions even with a two-thirds vote. I'm also weighing the fiscal side, where $8.4B in bonds means roughly $12 billion or more to repay over 20 to 25 years, with debt service taking top priority over other spending.

I'm now checking the case against the measure's design: the institute would be exempt from public records and open meetings laws, the bonds are a claim on roughly $12 billion in repayment, and the "pays for itself" claim doesn't hold up given CIRM's track record. I'm also weighing whether a separate $7.5B science bond on the 2028 ballot offers a better route, so voting no wouldn't close off state research funding.

I'm running through the rest of the case against: the newspaper editorial boards, columnists, and good-government and taxpayer groups on both sides who oppose it, plus Hoover's neutral analysis flagging real risks. I'm also noting that the 20% licensing discount could create perverse incentives and might be hard to enforce. On balance, the policy goal of funding immunology is worthy, but the governance and transparency problems with this particular vehicle look serious enough to weigh heavily toward "no."

I'm weighing whether to answer "no" alone, since the user asked for only yes or no, and whether giving a voting recommendation on a ballot measure is something I should do at all.

I'm weighing whether a plain "no" is the right answer here, since the user asked for only yes or no and I've already settled that the governance and fiscal problems with this measure outweigh its goal. The remaining question is whether recommending a vote on a ballot measure is something I should do at all, even though the criticism comes from across the political spectrum.

I'm going to run one more search to check for late developments, like a named director or amendments, that could change the picture before I settle on "no."

I'm checking whether any substantive rebuttal to the tailoring and transparency criticisms has appeared, such as a defense from the institute or its backers.

# Opinion: Vote No. Prop 38 Is an $8.4 billion Money Grab
Here are four reasons opponents say Prop 38 should be rejected:
**1.** **The billionaire’s research institute – CIII – doesn’t currently exist.** It has no director and no ongoing research projects.
We were not even able to identify a current address or phone number.
...
**2.** **No transparency and accountability?** Proposition 38 exempts CIII from state transparency and ethics laws, including the Public Records Act and open-meeting requirements.
It also exempts its decisionmakers from the Political Reform Act.
This means they will NOT be required to disclose personal assets and income for the purpose of avoiding conflicts of interest.
Why would we give $4.2 billion to an institute that is excused from standard accountability procedures?

# California Cancer Patients Divided Over Whether Prop 38 Will Help Them
## California cancer patients disagree over whether Proposition 38 will help them
Cancer patients who say their lives were saved by innovations in immunotherapy treatments are among the most vocal proponents of California’s Proposition 38, arguing the $8.4 billion bond measure to fund immune-system research would save even more lives.
But those who oppose Proposition 38 are also patients, who say their illnesses are being exploited to shill for an initiative that is overly narrow, opaque and expensive.
...
Backers of Proposition 38 proposed it as a solution to the Trump administration’s attack on science: where federal research funding has become diminished or uncertain, California would step in, issuing bond money to bring stability to promising projects and turn the state into a hub of excellence for immunology and immunotherapy research.

# Top immunology association divided over $8.4-billion California ballot measure to fund the field, emails show
## Half the money seems earmarked for a research center co-founded by Prop 38’s billionaire backer
The UCLA-affiliated California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.Courtesy Todd Chaney/UCLA
...
SAN DIEGO — Internal emails obtained by STAT show that the American Association of Immunologists, the field’s leading scientific society, is sharply divided over California’s Proposition 38, even though it would provide $8.4 billion in taxpayer dollars for the type of research its members do.
The emails show that the association’s policy and advocacy committee met in July and later recommended that the organization rescind its endorsement of the measure after learning that Prop 38 would likely yield a windfall for a research center co-founded by the billionaire philanthropist who is its leading backer.
But the association’s council, its governing body, voted in August to maintain the endorsement after meeting with the philanthropist, Gary Michelson.

I'm weighing the strongest argument for "yes" to be fair. Immunotherapy is a promising field, and $8.4B spread over roughly a decade would add about $840M a year, which is meaningful against NIH's overall budget and California's share of it.

Next I'm checking the federal funding angle: the Trump administration cut and froze grants, and although Congress restored most of the money, the uncertainty is still there. I'm also weighing whether the competitive grants half, which goes to UC campuses, Stanford, Caltech, Scripps, and others, could do real good even if the institute half is shaky. The cost is roughly $500 to 600 million a year, about a quarter of a percent of the general fund, and the endorsements from Newsom, both parties, patient groups, and immunologist and labor organizations point toward support.

Now I'm weighing the case against it: the measure would direct $4.2B to one unproven nonprofit tied to its main funder, with criteria that seem written around that single entity. The institute itself is barely operating so far, with only a handful of staff, no director, and an unfinished building.

The measure's design gives this nonprofit an unusual amount of power, including exemptions from the Public Records Act, open meetings law, and conflict-of-interest disclosure, along with a role in bond issuance, grant decisions, and licensing. Termination looks difficult too, and I'm checking how hard it would be to undo.

Now I'm going through the measure's remaining design problems: the grants council is made up of representatives from the same institutions that can receive grants, which creates self-dealing risk, and the Legislature can't amend the allocation provisions even with a two-thirds vote. I'm also weighing the fiscal side, where $8.4B in bonds means roughly $12 billion or more to repay over 20 to 25 years, with debt service taking top priority over other spending.

I'm now checking the case against the measure's design: the institute would be exempt from public records and open meetings laws, the bonds are a claim on roughly $12 billion in repayment, and the "pays for itself" claim doesn't hold up given CIRM's track record. I'm also weighing whether a separate $7.5B science bond on the 2028 ballot offers a better route, so voting no wouldn't close off state research funding.

I'm running through the rest of the case against: the newspaper editorial boards, columnists, and good-government and taxpayer groups on both sides who oppose it, plus Hoover's neutral analysis flagging real risks. I'm also noting that the 20% licensing discount could create perverse incentives and might be hard to enforce. On balance, the policy goal of funding immunology is worthy, but the governance and transparency problems with this particular vehicle look serious enough to weigh heavily toward "no."

I'm weighing whether to answer "no" alone, since the user asked for only yes or no, and whether giving a voting recommendation on a ballot measure is something I should do at all.

I'm weighing whether a plain "no" is the right answer here, since the user asked for only yes or no and I've already settled that the governance and fiscal problems with this measure outweigh its goal. The remaining question is whether recommending a vote on a ballot measure is something I should do at all, even though the criticism comes from across the political spectrum.

I'm going to run one more search to check for late developments, like a named director or amendments, that could change the picture before I settle on "no."

I'm checking whether any substantive rebuttal to the tailoring and transparency criticisms has appeared, such as a defense from the institute or its backers.

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.

Half the money seems earmarked for a research center co-founded by Prop 38’s billionaire backer

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.
SAN DIEGO — Internal emails obtained by STAT show that the American Association of Immunologists, the field’s leading scientific society, is sharply divided over California’s Proposition 38, even though it would provide $8.4 billion in taxpayer dollars for the type of research its members do.
The emails show that the association’s policy and advocacy committee met in July and later recommended that the organization rescind its endorsement of the measure after learning that Prop 38 would likely yield a windfall for a research center co-founded by the billionaire philanthropist who is its leading backer. But the association’s council, its governing body, voted in August to maintain the endorsement after meeting with the philanthropist, Gary Michelson.
Advertisement
In one email, AAI’s director of government affairs, Jacob Schumacher, wrote that five members of the association’s council voted to keep the endorsement, with one opposed and two abstentions. These details have not previously been made public, and a separate message from Schumacher indicates AAI, which has more than 7,700 members, did not plan to share them.

Is Prop. 38 unconstitutional? Opponents take immunology bond fight to AG
By Tarini Mehta
Updated October 8, 2026 11:13 AM
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Tuesday, Feb. 10, 2026, in Sacramento.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $38 million and spent nearly $20 million of it on television advertisements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-9WZJcETxc) in support of the $8.4 billion immunology research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html) on the November ballot.
The No on Proposition 38 group had raised less than $640 by Sept. 19. Instead of funding ads, the group is focused on letter-writing campaigns to highlight possible issues with the ballot initiative.
On Oct. 6, they wrote a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta alleging that the measure may violate the state constitution.
“The stakes are substantial,” committee co-chair David Panush wrote. “Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution. Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Supporters of the proposition, meanwhile, said the letter was a “campaign stunt to distract voters.”
The proposition will ask voters to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of research grants — many of which were later restored, but not without creating disruptions and delays. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) appeared to meet the criteria for half of the immunology bond’s funds: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Prop. 38.
Last month, the opponents sent a letter to the UC Board of Regents urging them to only approve additional funding or construction commitments for the CIII if it agrees to public transparency and conflict-of-interest safeguards that public agencies are subject to. The UC board approved next steps in the construction of the institute’s facility at its September meeting.
Violation of constitution?
In a letter this week, Panush urged Bonta to weigh in on if Prop. 38 violates the California Constitution before voters decide to approve it. The attorney general is involved in the ballot initiative process in California from the very beginning. For any initiative proposed by citizens to make it onto the ballot, it must first be submitted to the attorney general with a request to prepare a title and summary that can be circulated to collect signatures — a step that was taken months ago for the immunology bond.
Suggesting Bonta take another look at the measure, Panush cited a section of the California Constitution that says an initiative that identifies a private corporation to perform any function or have any power may not be submitted to voters. While Prop. 38 does not name any private corporation, he asked if it “makes any legal difference when the requirements effectively identify it.”
For the institute that will receive half the bond proceeds if Prop. 38 passes, the measure outlined several specific requirements. The nonprofit immunology research institute must be affiliated with a University of California campus that has a hospital and clinic volume of more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year. It must also own or lease a site that is at least 200,000 square feet in size and note philanthropic funding of at least $250 million in its affiliation agreement with the UC. And it must have secured $50 million to support a rapid vaccine development program and another $50 million for a microbiome research program.
“That would mean an institute connected to a health system with, say, 3 million visits, or occupying 180,000 square feet, would be excluded regardless of its research capabilities,” Panush said. “These thresholds operate as categorical exclusions, not measures of an institute’s scientific merit.”
In a previous interview with The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), a spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health. If the state is unable to identify a suitable institute, it can modify the criteria, per the measure.
In its affiliation agreement with the UC, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is described as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation” governed independently of the university. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open “in a year or so,” according to Yes on Proposition 38 spokesperson Robin Swanson. The institute is operational and has already administered grants, she said. A UC report indicates that construction will be complete by the end of 2028.
The UC, which sponsored a law to place a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317049270.html) on the March 2028 ballot, said it does not have position on Prop. 38.
‘Saved my life’
For the supporters of the measure, the central campaign message has been that it will provide critical funding for time-sensitive immunology research. This includes finding cures for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
“Prop 38 will provide much-needed funding to accelerate medical research at California’s world-class universities and research institutes, which is desperately needed in the face of federal research cuts,” Swanson said.
In a moving advertisement, cancer survivor Andrew Dale says immunotherapy saved his life and allowed him to see his daughter graduate from high school. Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor who spoke with The Bee last month, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317199654.html), but the country and the whole world.
The measure is supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association. It also has the endorsement of the California Republican Party and the California Democratic Party. The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign contributed $250,000 to the Democratic Party in September.
The campaign had raised more than $38 million, as of Sept. 19, of which more than $33 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy. Another $5 million was donated by Meyer Luskin, co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy.
The campaign has spent nearly $20 million on cable airtime and advertisement production costs. It also spent more than $10 million earlier this year to circulate its petition and collect enough signatures to get onto the ballot.
