Retired government analysts raise alarm on immunology bond on November ballot
By Tarini Mehta
September 11, 2026 3:33 PM
Ballots are dropped off at a polling location on Fountain Square Drive in Citrus Heights on Election Day, June 2, 2026.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Three former employees of the California Legislative Analyst’s Office came out in strong opposition against Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316259099.html) Thursday, arguing that the ballot measure that seeks to support medical research lacked appropriate provisions for transparency and accountability. Instead, they said, it seemed to “steer public funds” to its billionaire backer’s “philanthropic project” and then “hide its tracks.”
The proposition (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) will ask voters in the November election to allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
Its backers say the measure materialized as a response to the Trump administration’s cuts and freezes to thousands of medical research grants in recent months. The stated goal is to allow immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s to advance unimpeded. Half of the bond proceeds would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, while the rest would be distributed as competitive research grants to public or nonprofit universities and institutions.
Earlier this summer, CalMatters reported only one research institute in California appeared (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) to meet the criteria included in the measure for the nonprofit that would be awarded half the bond proceeds. That institute is the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, an independent medical research organization affiliated with UCLA. Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist and medical inventor, is both the co-founder of that institute and the chief backer of Proposition 38.
‘Hides its tracks’
“Those of you who have worked with the Legislative Analyst’s Office before, you know how reticent our staff is to ever engage in partisan political debates,” said Marianne O’Malley, former managing principal analyst at the LAO, at a virtual news conference organized by the No on Proposition 38 campaign Thursday. “We don’t do that, so you may be wondering why three retired LAO staffers are talking publicly about Proposition 38. The reason is this is no ordinary measure. This measure hijacks the initiative process to steer public funds to a billionaire’s philanthropic project, and then it hides its tracks by waiving all the usual laws to promote governmental transparency.”
O’Malley said it is not uncommon for the government to transfer funds to a nonprofit or private entity to carry out a project. However, such a transfer usually follows an open and competitive bidding process — something Proposition 38 does not seem to do, she said.
Robin Swanson, spokesperson for the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign, said the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy very likely meets the criteria, but the ultimate decision will be taken by the California Department of Public Health.
Swanson said the measure was written to allocate funds to an institute that is “ready to go, competitive and world-class.” She said state bond measures cannot designate funding to a specific nonprofit, but they can establish criteria to ensure the most qualified entities are eligible. First announced in 2024, the CIII is currently under construction and scheduled to open soon.
“We don’t have time to wait. Patients don’t have time to wait for another entity to be created,” Swanson said. “We want an institute that’s able to scale and quickly turn research into life-saving cures.”
For O’Malley, the problem with the measure does not end with the selection of the institute. She said Proposition 38 did not have provisions to promote transparency after the money is disbursed. She pointed to a clause that said the chosen nonprofit institute was not to be deemed a public agency. Therefore, it would be immune from public records and open meeting requirements that ordinarily provide accountability over public funds.
Will it pay for itself?
The backers of Proposition 38 argue that it has strong accountability protections, including independent financial audits, annual reports, a citizens’ oversight committee and a 2% cap on state administrative costs, apart from the general transparency rules that all nonprofits must follow.
They also say the measure protects taxpayers and is designed to pay for itself, since 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the total costs of the bond. With the global immunotherapy market projected to grow rapidly over the next decade, supporters believe the research program created under Proposition 38 will create “more than enough revenue.” In addition, treatments developed through funded research are to be offered at a 20% discount in California.
However, Dan Carson, also a former LAO analyst, disputed that claim based on California’s experience with stem-cell research bonds passed in 2004 and 2020. In 2004, voters approved Proposition 71, creating the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine and authorizing $3 billion in bond funding for stem cell research. Californians approved an additional $5.5 billion for the institute in 2020.
During his time at the LAO, Carson said he worked on a team that analyzed Proposition 71 and found that it had failed to deliver on the huge financial windfall it had promised the state.
“The state eventually received only a tiny fraction of the billions of dollars we were promised,” he said. “We got about $16 million in payoff for intellectual property, and we were projected to spend about $6 billion over time to repay the principal and interest on those bonds. So here we go again with Prop. 38. This time, an even bigger $8.4 billion medical research bond issue that will cost us roughly half a billion dollars a year for decades to pay off.”
The research topics eligible for funding under the bond measure include understanding disease formation and factors that contribute to the same. While those research activities are important, Carson said, they do not directly develop new cures that can generate assets to pay off the bond costs. However, the measure does ask that projects with the “greatest potential for yielding the most immediate, accessible and affordable therapies” be prioritized in the competitive research grant selections.
Loading…
‘Institutional favoritism’
Those selections, for the half of the money that will not go to the single institute, will be made by a council consisting of representatives of the University of California campuses, nonprofit universities and research institutions in consultation with the selected institute. The grants will be awarded to universities and institutions represented on the council.
According to Judy Heiman, former principal analyst at the LAO, that creates a conflict of interest which will result in members of a closed group discussing how to divide up $4.2 billion amongst themselves rather than finding the best uses for the money.
“There’s a legitimate argument about whether California should add billions of dollars in medical research spending to its already substantial debt burden,” Heiman said. “Those who think we shouldn’t will vote against Prop. 38. I would argue that even those who would like to see a major state investment in research should vote no on Prop. 38 and demand an open, transparent and accountable structure. Scientific merit, not institutional favoritism, should drive where the money goes.”
The No on Proposition 38 campaign, led by Stanford Universitysenior scholar Robert Kaplan (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article315629674.html), has so far not reported any contributions. Kaplan has consistently criticized the practice of funding research focused on specific diseases rather than investing in medical research more broadly, especially when the Trump administration’s cuts affected public health programs across the board.
Support for Prop. 38
The Yes on Proposition 38 campaign has raised more than $27 million so far, of which more than $22 million has come from billionaire philanthropist Gary Michelson and his nonprofit Michelson Center for Public Policy.
The measure has the endorsement of the California Democratic Party and the California Republican Party. It is also supported by a broad coalition of doctors, nurses and patient advocates. This includes the Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, American Nurses Association California, Prostate Cancer Foundation and Kidney Cancer Association.
Laurie Adami, a cancer survivor whose life was saved by an immunotherapy clinical trial at UCLA, said Prop. 38 will benefit not just California, but the country and the whole world.
“I lived through struggling to find new treatments for 12 years. I had heard about CAR T-cell therapy in 2012, but I had to wait six years for it to make it into trial because these things are not enough of a priority,” Adami said. “Everybody says the federal government will restore (research funding). I’m sorry, patients can’t wait for that, just like I couldn’t. If my trial hadn’t opened, I was a month away from dying. That’s how sick I was, and this is the case for too many people.”
In November, Prop. 38 will need “yes” votes from a majority of California voters to be approved.

by
Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/)

In summary
Proposition 38 is written in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It will appear on the November ballot as Proposition 38 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf), which would provide $8.4 billion for cutting edge immunology research and cures for heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer’s, as well as other diseases that may be vanquished with immunotherapies.
Included in that is more than $4 billion for one, unnamed institute. The legal language behind the proposition gives no outward indication where that $4 billion would go other than pages of oddly specific language that outlines the parameters the lucky recipient must meet to qualify for the windfall.
That might not mean much to the average voter who is trying to parse 14 propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) as they fill out their ballots.
But a CalMatters analysis shows that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition.
The analysis raises the question of why the framers took such care to construct a highly specific set of criteria that seemingly points to a single eligible institute without naming it in the bond.
READ NEXT
He spent decades researching dementia. Trump’s DEI purge killed his grant, and dozens more (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2025/04/health-research/)
April 10, 2025 April 10, 2025
“It is very clearly designed to support a specific nonprofit,” said Sarah Hill, a professor of political science at Cal State Fullerton who studies California’s ballot process. She said Prop. 38’s language is “oddly specific with numbers,” which on its own should raise the suspicion of voters.
“Why is it just this one institute that you have designated that’s going to get half the money?” she asked, posing a question she believes voters too will wonder.
The split design of the bond measure might also trouble voters, Hill added. As written, the bond measure would mete out more than $4 billion to one unnamed institute and over $4 billion to select nonprofit and public university researchers who apply for grants on a competitive basis.
It’s as if the bond backers are saying, “it’s OK that some of it is going to a specific nonprofit because the rest is much broader, much more general,” Hill said. “They’re trying to get people to focus there, but would half of the money still be designated for one nonprofit? Essentially, yes.”
Hill doesn’t know why the bond measure’s backers are hopeful it’ll pass. One possible reason she gave: Enough voters won’t scrutinize this thoroughly and they’ll support it because it promotes medical research into recognizable diseases.
“They’re hoping the way this goes, the voters will just think it sounds nice, which sometimes works,” she added.
There’s recent history that a confusing ballot measure targeting just one entity passes, albeit barely. In 2024 voters approved Proposition 34 by 50.9%. It placed limits on how health care providers spend money. Never explicitly mentioned in the measure’s text was that it appeared to apply to only one organization (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/11/california-election-results-prop-34-health-care-spending/): the AIDS Healthcare Foundation.

Δ
Backer of bond is also co-founder of immunology institute
The billionaire (https://www.forbes.com/profile/gary-michelson/) co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, Gary K. Michelson, is one of the two ultrawealthy chief backers of Proposition 38 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf). The institute first became a nonprofit in 2022. Michelson has given it at least $120 million since then. Michelson is the board chair of the institute, which is housed at a research center owned by UCLA (https://www3.research.ucla.edu/research-park).
Prop. 38’s language allocates half the bond money to one unnamed nonprofit that must meet very specific criteria:
It’s a nonprofit founded before 2025;
It focuses on immunology and immunotherapy research rather than research broadly;
It’s affiliated with a University of California campus with a medical center that serves a minimum number of patients. Currently only UCLA meets that threshold;
It must meet a minimum square footage requirement for the size of the research institute;
It received a minimum dollar amount in donations from funders, including for specific research endeavors.
A UCLA spokesperson, Phil Hampton, confirmed that among all nonprofit entities affiliated with UCLA, only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy could satisfy the stipulations of Prop. 38.
The website (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) supporting the proposition touts it as an effort to award grant dollars to scientists working on drug therapies for incurable diseases, but makes no mention of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy as a likely recipient of half the bond revenue. Michelson and a nonprofit that he founded, the Michelson Center For Public Policy, donated (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1485847&view=late1) at least $8.2 million to the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign. Another campaign donor and institute co-founder, Meyer Luskin, has given (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1485847&view=late1) at least $5 million.
A former science research administrator publicly opposes the proposition. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federally funded National Institutes of Health — the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research. He said concentrating half the funding to one unnamed institute is unfair. “There is a lot of talent in immunology, immunotherapy research in California,” he said in an interview. “All the institutions are scrambling, and so tracking a huge portion of it to one institution, I think, is a bad idea.”
Kaplan also worries the bond measure is too focused on one discipline —immunotherapy — at theexpense of a wider array of biomedical research (https://amp.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article315629674.html). He’s currently a senior scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine’s Clinical Excellence Research Center.
The Michelson Center for Public Policy, where Michelson is the director, has given (https://calmatters.org/about/funding/#:~:text=Michelson%20Center%20for%20Public%20Policy) between $1,000 and $9,900 to CalMatters.
The potential for cures through immunotherapies is huge because most diseases involve the immune system, the bond measure backers say. California science research has been rocked by funding cuts ordered by the White House that led to hundreds of cancelled federal grants. While many of those grants were restored (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/), the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign says ongoing federal funding instability necessitates state investment in immunology and immunotherapies.
Should Prop. 38 pass, bond payments will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250488.pdf), bringing the cost of the $8.4 billion bond to more than $12 billion, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The office said costs to the state may be less if the drug therapies developed through the bond’s research funding generate profits that are then routed back to California’s coffers.
What bond backer says
CalMatters presented its findings to the The Yes on 38 (https://yeson38.com/) campaign. In a lengthy email response, Claudia Briggs, the campaign’s spokesperson, said Prop. 38’s language isn’t uniquely tailored to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. She defended the detailed eligibility criteria written into the bond proposition.
“We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding,” she wrote. “We can’t speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify across California.”
Briggs wrote that the eligibility criteria were “intentionally designed to ensure that whichever institute is selected is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
She explained that the eligibility criteria were crafted to “ensure the selected institute is primarily focused on immunology and immunotherapy research, already has significant resources before receiving bond funds, has an adequate physical facility to accommodate multiple labs and research programs, and has an existing close working relationship with at least one UC campus in order to establish the foundation for the cross-collaboration that will be important to the success of the measure.”
Drugs created through research funded by the bond would have to be discounted at 20% for California residents and 10% of any revenue from the drugs developed through bond-funded research would go back to the state’s general fund. If the revenues repay what the state spent on the bond and there’s money left over (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=13), the spare cash would return to the special account supporting the goals of the bond.
The bond measure language says that if no institute qualifies, the California Department of Public Health can adjust the criteria to select a winning institute.
How the bond seemingly points to one institute
The bond proposition language says that the institute receiving the $4.2 billion must be affiliated with a University of California campus housing a medical center with more than 3.5 million outpatient visitors and at least 35,000 inpatient admissions.
According to the UC’s latest fiscal audit (https://www.ucop.edu/uc-controller/financial-reports/systemwide-reports/medical-center-reports/24-25/medical-center-report-2025.pdf#page=30), only the UCLA medical center and its affiliated sites registered more than 3.5 million outpatient visits in 2025, with 4.1 million visits. UC San Francisco came in second with 3.4 million visits. UCLA’s website says its medical system admits at least 46,000 people for inpatient care (https://www.uclahealth.org/discover/about).
Based on that criteria, only an institute affiliated with UCLA is presently eligible for the $4.2 billion fund.
The bond measure also requires that the research entity measures at least 200,000 square feet and has a “primary” purpose of “conducting research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy.” Press releases (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/michelsons-give-120-million-gift-to-ucla-immunology-immunotherapy) from 2024indicate (https://www.michelsonmedicalresearch.org/news/california-institute-for-immunology-and-immunotherapy-new-ucla-research-park) that the institute will occupy between 360,000 and 500,000 square feet of space on UCLA-owned property.
The institute’s stated purpose is to be an (https://www.calimmunology.org/) “invention factory” for “life-saving drugs, vaccines, diagnostics” and to “end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” It initially received (https://www.michelsonmedicalresearch.org/news/ucla-receives-120-million-gift-from-alya-and-gary-michelson-ciii#:~:text=%24200%20million%20appropriation%20from%20the%20state%20of%20California) $200 million in support from the state budget that helped to secure (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/california-legislature-first-day/#:~:text=In%20other%20higher%20education%20news%3A) the UCLA research space.
One of the other requirements of Prop. 38 is that the nonprofit receiving the $4.2 billion be an entity that’s received at least $250 million in philanthropic support. The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy has received a reported $250 million (https://labusinessjournal.com/special-reports/bioscience-institute-takes-shape/#:~:text=Private%20donation%20commitments%20have%20totaled%20%24250%20million%20to%20date%2C%20primarily%20from%20the%20six%2Dmember%20board.).
Another bond measure requirement is that top officials from the affiliated UC campus sit on the unnamed institute’s board (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=7). Four top UCLA administrators are listed on the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy’s board of directors, including the campus chancellor, Julio Frenk, and the school’s vice chancellor for research, Roger Wakimoto. The institute’s webpage, labeled “Board of Directors,” lists the senior UCLA personnel as “UCLA Board of Directors.” At least four UCLA officials must sit on the institute’s fiduciary board, according to a 2023 term sheet (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/aug23/h3attach1.pdf#page=3)of the affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute. The UCLA personnel are named as directors in the institute’s most recent Form 990 tax filing (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093/202631219349301013/full).
Prop. 38 is highly specific about two donations that must be at least $50 million each that seem to only apply to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The bond language says one donation is to support “a rapid vaccine development program” and the other supports “a microbiome research program.”
Michelson and his wife donated $50 million to two research programs with near-verbatim descriptions that match the bond language as part of their $120 million contribution to the institute, according toa press release (https://www.garykmichelson.org/blog/ucla-receives-120-million-gift-from-alya-and-gary-michelson-for-new-california-institute-for-immunology-amp-immunotherapy). The microbiome research will be conducted in collaboration with the UCLA Goodman-Luskin Microbiome Center, which Luskin and his wife helped establish through a $20 million donation they made with another couple (https://www.uclahealth.org/news/release/ucla-receives-20-million-establish-goodman-luskin-microbiome).
Other grants limited to select researchers
While an unnamed institute is to receive half the money from Prop. 38, the other half will be meted out to a narrow array of public and nonprofit-based researchers in California through a competitive grant application process.
A council selected by the chancellors of seven of the 10 UC campuses, officials from other universities and nonprofit researchers will select the winning grant proposals (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=10). The three UC

This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it?

By Mikhail Zinshteyn, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

It will appear on the November ballot as Proposition 38, which would provide $8.4 billion for cutting edge immunology research and cures for heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer’s, as well as other diseases that may be vanquished with immunotherapies.

Included in that is more than $4 billion for one, unnamed institute. The legal language behind the proposition gives no outward indication where that $4 billion would go other than pages of oddly specific language that outlines the parameters the lucky recipient must meet to qualify for the windfall.

That might not mean much to the average voter who is trying to parse 14 propositions as they fill out their ballots.

But a CalMatters analysis shows that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition.

The analysis raises the question of why the framers took such care to construct a highly specific set of criteria that seemingly points to a single eligible institute without naming it in the bond.

“It is very clearly designed to support a specific nonprofit,” said Sarah Hill, a professor of political science at Cal State Fullerton who studies California’s ballot process. She said Prop. 38’s language is “oddly specific with numbers,” which on its own should raise the suspicion of voters.

“Why is it just this one institute that you have designated that's going to get half the money?” she asked, posing a question she believes voters too will wonder.

The split design of the bond measure might also trouble voters, Hill added. As written, the bond measure would mete out more than $4 billion to one unnamed institute and over $4 billion to select nonprofit and public university researchers who apply for grants on a competitive basis. 

It’s as if the bond backers are saying, “it's OK that some of it is going to a specific nonprofit because the rest is much broader, much more general,” Hill said. “They're trying to get people to focus there, but would half of the money still be designated for one nonprofit? Essentially, yes.”

Hill doesn’t know why the bond measure’s backers are hopeful it’ll pass. One possible reason she gave: Enough voters won’t scrutinize this thoroughly and they’ll support it because it promotes medical research into recognizable diseases. 

“They're hoping the way this goes, the voters will just think it sounds nice, which sometimes works,” she added.

There’s recent history that a confusing ballot measure targeting just one entity passes, albeit barely. In 2024 voters approved Proposition 34 by 50.9%. It placed limits on how health care providers spend money. Never explicitly mentioned in the measure’s text was that it appeared to apply to only one organization: the AIDS Healthcare Foundation.

Backer of bond is also co-founder of immunology institute

The billionaire co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, Gary K. Michelson, is one of the two ultrawealthy chief backers of Proposition 38. The institute first became a nonprofit in 2022. Michelson has given it at least $120 million since then. Michelson is the board chair of the institute, which is housed at a research center owned by UCLA. 

Prop. 38’s language allocates half the bond money to one unnamed nonprofit that must meet very specific criteria: 

  • It’s a nonprofit founded before 2025;
  • It focuses on immunology and immunotherapy research rather than research broadly;
  • It’s affiliated with a University of California campus with a medical center that serves a minimum number of patients. Currently only UCLA meets that threshold; 
  • It must meet a minimum square footage requirement for the size of the research institute;
  • It received a minimum dollar amount in donations from funders, including for specific research endeavors. 

A UCLA spokesperson, Phil Hampton, confirmed that among all nonprofit entities affiliated with UCLA, only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy could satisfy the stipulations of Prop. 38. 

The website supporting the proposition touts it as an effort to award grant dollars to scientists working on drug therapies for incurable diseases, but makes no mention of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy as a likely recipient of half the bond revenue. Michelson and a nonprofit that he founded, the Michelson Center For Public Policy, donated at least $8.2 million to the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign. Another campaign donor and institute co-founder, Meyer Luskin, has given at least $5 million.

A former science research administrator publicly opposes the proposition. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federally funded National Institutes of Health — the world's largest public funder of biomedical research. He said concentrating half the funding to one unnamed institute is unfair. "There is a lot of talent in immunology, immunotherapy research in California," he said in an interview. "All the institutions are scrambling, and so tracking a huge portion of it to one institution, I think, is a bad idea." 

Kaplan also worries the bond measure is too focused on one discipline —immunotherapy — at the expense of a wider array of biomedical research. He's currently a senior scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine’s Clinical Excellence Research Center.

The Michelson Center for Public Policy, where Michelson is the director, has given between $1,000 and $9,900 to CalMatters.

The potential for cures through immunotherapies is huge because most diseases involve the immune system, the bond measure backers say. California science research has been rocked by funding cuts ordered by the White House that led to hundreds of cancelled federal grants. While many of those grants were restored, the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign says ongoing federal funding instability necessitates state investment in immunology and immunotherapies.

Should Prop. 38 pass, bond payments will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years, bringing the cost of the $8.4 billion bond to more than $12 billion, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The office said costs to the state may be less if the drug therapies developed through the bond’s research funding generate profits that are then routed back to California’s coffers.

What bond backer says

CalMatters presented its findings to the The Yes on 38 campaign. In a lengthy email response, Claudia Briggs, the campaign’s spokesperson, said Prop. 38’s language isn’t uniquely tailored to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. She defended the detailed eligibility criteria written into the bond proposition.

“We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding,” she wrote. “We can’t speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify across California.”

Briggs wrote that the eligibility criteria were “intentionally designed to ensure that whichever institute is selected is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”

She explained that the eligibility criteria were crafted to “ensure the selected institute is primarily focused on immunology and immunotherapy research, already has significant resources before receiving bond funds, has an adequate physical facility to accommodate multiple labs and research programs, and has an existing close working relationship with at least one UC campus in order to establish the foundation for the cross-collaboration that will be important to the success of the measure.”

Drugs created through research funded by the bond would have to be discounted at 20% for California residents and 10% of any revenue from the drugs developed through bond-funded research would go back to the state’s general fund. If the revenues repay what the state spent on the bond and there’s money left over, the spare cash would return to the special account supporting the goals of the bond. 

The bond measure language says that if no institute qualifies, the California Department of Public Health can adjust the criteria to select a winning institute. 

How the bond seemingly points to one institute

The bond proposition language says that the institute receiving the $4.2 billion must be affiliated with a University of California campus housing a medical center with more than 3.5 million outpatient visitors and at least 35,000 inpatient admissions.

According to the UC’s latest fiscal audit, only the UCLA medical center and its affiliated sites registered more than 3.5 million outpatient visits in 2025, with 4.1 million visits. UC San Francisco came in second with 3.4 million visits. UCLA’s website says its medical system admits at least 46,000 people for inpatient care.

Based on that criteria, only an institute affiliated with UCLA is presently eligible for the $4.2 billion fund. 

The bond measure also requires that the research entity measures at least 200,000 square feet and has a “primary” purpose of “conducting research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy.” Press releases from 2024 indicate that the institute will occupy between 360,000 and 500,000 square feet of space on UCLA-owned property. 

The institute's stated purpose is to be an “invention factory” for “life-saving drugs, vaccines, diagnostics” and to “end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” It initially received $200 million in support from the state budget that helped to secure the UCLA research space. 

One of the other requirements of Prop. 38 is that the nonprofit receiving the $4.2 billion be an entity that’s received at least $250 million in philanthropic support. The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy has received a reported $250 million.

Who doesn’t want to cure cancer and save the state’s budget in the process?
But Prop 38 is no balm; it’s one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years.
The measure requires the California Department of Public Health to give half the bond money — $4.2 billion — to an unnamed nonprofit medical research institute that meets a long and unusual list of criteria, including occupying a minimum 200,000-square-foot space and receiving a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
These requirements have no bearing on an institution’s ability to conduct high-quality, cutting-edge immunology research. Instead, they’re written so that a lone research center is eligible to receive (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) the lion’s share of taxpayer money: the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California has many established and well-regarded research institutes — including some that have made significant advances in these fields.
But the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy is not among them.
Instead, it’s a brand-new institute, and its founders include the same billionaires who paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and financier Michael Milken, who, in addition to his longtime financing of medical research, (https://milkeninstitute.org/speakers/michael-milken-5) is also known as the “junk bond king.” He was pardoned by President Donald Trump in 2020 (https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/18/trump-pardons-michael-milken-face-of-1980s-financial-scandals.html) for his 1990 guilty plea to racketeering and securities fraud.
In an endorsement interview, Yes on 38 campaign spokesperson Robin Swanson insisted to us that the institute is “well positioned” to put $4.2 billion to good use, touting initial philanthropic contributions of $250 million (https://labusinessjournal.com/special-reports/bioscience-institute-takes-shape/#:~:text=Private%20donation%20commitments%20have%20totaled%20%24250%20million%20to%20date%2C%20primarily%20from%20the%20six%2Dmember%20board.) and its affiliation with UCLA and its medical center.
But the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy literally has no track record of developing, funding or bringing medical research to market. It isn’t even fully built. Despite already receiving $200 million in taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park) in California’s 2022-2023 budget (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2022-23/pdf/Enacted/BudgetSummary/HigherEducation.pdf), construction on a “majority” of the space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028, a spokesperson acknowledged via email.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Key leadership positions remain empty. As of this writing, the institute is still searching for a director, the spokesperson said.
It doesn’t even have a public strategic plan (https://www.calimmunology.org/about). When we pressed for details, the spokesperson would only say, “While CIII continues to refine its longer-term business plan, several core elements are complete or well underway.”
The spokesperson insisted that the institute wasn’t involved in drafting Prop 38 and isn’t part of the campaign. But, again, its billionaire co-founders put the measure on the ballot and have raised more than $38 million to support it (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
The institute may be playing coy about how it will benefit from Prop 38, but campaign proponents make no secret of where the money will end up.
“CIII is ready to go,” Swanson said, against all evidence.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Swanson and other Prop 38 supporters leaned heavily on the UCLA affiliation to assuage concerns over the institute’s glaring shortcomings.
UCLA is indeed a top research university. But what exactly is the “affiliation” here?
The institute is leasing space at a new UCLA Research Park (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) but will mostly operate independently from the university. An institute spokesperson said the “formal affiliation agreement” defines their “relationship and responsibilities,” including mission and purpose, facilities, funding, intellectual property, personnel and governance. Some senior UCLA leaders sit on the institute’s board of directors (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors), including Chancellor Julio Frenk, and UCLA “reserves the right to veto actions that it deems will result in reputational harm or contravene the university’s mission,” Phil Hampton, senior director of communications for UCLA Health and the David Geffen School of Medicine, said in an email.
These vague answers do not assuage our serious doubts about the institute’s ability to manage billions in taxpayer funds.
Indeed, the measure also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through Prop 38-funded research — even therapies created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Funding decisions would be made by a council of representatives from seven of the 10 University of California campuses — Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco — and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions.
But there are red flags here, as well.
The money is reserved for projects at the institutions represented on the council — raising serious conflict-of-interest concerns. (Proponents said council members would have to abide by ethics and conflict-of-interest regulations — although the measure carves out multiple exceptions — and the council and institute would be subject to independent audits and annual reporting requirements.)
Supporters ask voters to look past these issues by arguing that state-level investment is needed because of President Donald Trump’s funding cuts for medical research. But National Institutes of Health funding for immunotherapy research has steadily risen since 2019 (https://report.nih.gov/funding/categorical-spending#/), when it was established as a new category.
Moreover, Robert Kaplan, an opponent of the measure who was an associate director at the National Institutes of Health and formerly led UCLA’s health services program, told us that Prop 38 fundamentally misunderstands how funding top-tier medical research works.
It doesn’t make sense to restrict billions of dollars to just one area of research, Kaplan said. After all, there’s no guarantee that immunology, as opposed to another field of study, holds the cure to cancer or Alzheimer’s. Funding should be prioritized for thoroughly vetted projects that show the greatest promise of making a difference. Limiting the eligibility pool will almost certainly waste money on efforts that lack merit or scientific rigor.
That’s a lesson Californians should be familiar with.
In 2004, voters approved $3 billion in bonds for stem-cell research, swayed by the promise of miracle cures and huge financial windfalls for the state. Those didn’t materialize, a Chronicle investigation found (https://projects.sfchronicle.com/2018/stem-cells/politics/?_gl=1*76rb29*_gcl_aw*R0NMLjE3OTAxMTQ1MzUuQ2owS0NRand6c2pWQmhDM0FSSXNBTG5NdjRuS1U2OEx6Z3BLUndsckVzczNmZTNRNXlnVzNYeFI1VUprUDZqcXljR3h5SzFEQzg2QXBDSWFBa1RLRUFMd193Y0I.*_gcl_au*MTYxMzIzNzI3Mi4xNzg4OTExNzQ5*_ga*MTQ1MTQ5NDU3MS4xNzgxMTM0OTQ4*_ga_56G0ZT3ZD0*czE3OTA4MDgxMDkkbzExNCRnMSR0MTc5MDgwODg5MCRqNjAkbDAkaDA.); in fact, the measure may have actually empowered an uptick in clinics peddling pseudoscience.
That didn’t stop voters from approving yet another measure in 2020 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-Prop-14-no-need-to-15592513.php) authorizing $5.5 billion in bonds for stem-cell research.

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
Let’s not make the same mistake a third time.
There isn’t a family in California who hasn’t been touched by cancer, Alzheimer’s or heart disease. Better treatments and cures cannot come fast enough. We applaud any billionaire who earnestly wants to harness their fortune to fight disease. But if Michelson, Luskin and Milken want Californians to believe that’s their intention with Prop 38, they should spend their own money and come back to taxpayers when their institute actually has some progress to show.

Opinion (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/) // Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/)
This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.
About Opinion
Guest opinions in Open Forum and Insight are produced by writers with expertise, personal experience or original insights on a subject of interest to our readers. Their views do not necessarily reflect the opinion of The Chronicle editorial board, which is committed to providing a diversity of ideas to our readership.
Read more about our transparency and ethics policies (https://www.sfchronicle.com/standards/)
And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.

Why is it the best solution to that problem?
Prop. 38 makes a long-term investment in one of the most promising areas of medical science: immunology, which harnesses the body’s own immune system to prevent, treat and cure devastating diseases.
Immunotherapies are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Patients who have been weeks away from dying have received breakthrough treatments that have led to long-term remission.
Prop. 38 brings together California’s world-class universities, nonprofit research institutions and leading scientists in a statewide effort to accelerate breakthrough immunology research, while providing stable funding at a time when federal research dollars are shrinking and increasingly uncertain.
Prop. 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others.
Why should California taxpayers take on $8.4 billion in debt for medical research?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers. It requires 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies be returned to California to offset the full cost of the bond, including interest.
Prop. 38 mandates that new treatments and cures developed under Prop. 38 be offered to Californians at 20% below the national average.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term health care expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Public funding of medical research has always been a central component of advancements in medicine. Of new drugs approved by the FDA between 2010 and 2019, 99.4% were the result of publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 also includes strong accountability provisions such as annual audits and limiting state administrative costs to no more than 2%.
With the federal government and private companies already spending billions on medical research, why does California need to step in?
Billions in funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health and other federal partners are already putting critical research for cures at risk.
Private companies tend to invest where they see the clearest path to profit, which can leave promising but high-risk research underfunded — especially early-stage work, rare diseases and treatments that may take years to develop. Public investment is essential in filling that gap. It allows scientists to pursue breakthroughs based on scientific promise and medical need, not just commercial potential, and helps move discoveries far enough along to attract additional investment.
The fact is, those suffering from debilitating diseases can’t afford to wait for the market alone to deliver, or wait on the federal government to fund this research. California can continue to lead the way in breakthrough medical research and the development of cures with Prop. 38.
What happens if the research fails to find any new, profitable treatments?
The field of immunology and immunotherapies has already proved to be incredibly promising. Breakthrough immunotherapies have already been developed and approved to prevent and fight cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas, and more.
The global immunotherapy market was valued at about $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow rapidly, reaching $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.

We believe California voters deserve a choice about investing in the future of scientific research and breakthroughs in our state. Prop. 38 puts that decision directly in the hands of voters, while requiring strong accountability for how the money is spent.
Prop. 38 provides the stable, long-term funding scientists need to pursue promising research without being dependent on changing political priorities or annual budget decisions, particularly as billions in federal research funding is being delayed and eliminated.
People who are living with debilitating diseases don’t have years to wait for the state or federal government to take action on this issue. We owe it to them to make this investment now by voting “yes” on Prop. 38.
What are the projected economic benefits and costs for lower-income households, small business owners and California taxpayers?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself. Ten percent of proceeds from licensing successful immunotherapies must be returned to California to offset the cost of the bonds, including principal and interest.
The global immunotherapy market was already valued at approximately $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California, home to many of the world’s leading scientists and research institutions, to lead that rapidly growing field.
There are also potentially enormous savings from preventing and curing diseases that currently cost families and our healthcare system tens of billions of dollars.
Prop. 38 includes another important protection for Californians: treatments and technologies developed through this publicly funded research must be offered in California at prices at least 20% below the national average.
Californians are investing in the research, and they should share in its benefits.
Why should Californians lock up $500 million per year of their state’s General Fund because of a ballot initiative backed by a billionaire whose institute receives half of the bond money?
That characterization ignores both what Prop. 38 actually does and what Californians get in return. For starters, finding treatments and cures to the most debilitating and costly diseases will save billions in avoided health expenses.
Prop. 38 will bring further investment into our state, creating billions of dollars in economic benefits and tens of thousands of good-paying jobs. Scientific research is an economic engine in California, and studies show that each dollar invested in medical research brings three dollars back into the economy.
And Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself while helping California lead a global immunotherapy market projected to reach $1.3 trillion by 2033.
The measure also contains strong taxpayer protections. Administrative costs are capped at 2%. Funds are tracked and audited. And 10% of licensing proceeds from successful therapies must be returned to California to help repay both the principal and interest on the bonds.
What proofs of concept is this ballot measure modeled on? When has California or another state achieved success with a similar plan?
We already know immunotherapy works. Breakthrough immunotherapies have been developed and approved to prevent and fight melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas and other cancers.
The opportunity now is to accelerate that progress and apply the science of the immune system to an even broader range of diseases.
Prop. 38 combines sustained funding with a statewide network so California’s leading scientists can collaborate, share sophisticated research infrastructure and move promising discoveries toward patients faster.
California has led medical innovation before. Prop. 38 gives us the opportunity to do it again.
Why restrict this to immunology rather than giving program managers more discretion, like DARPA does, to pick the most promising investments as evidence and trends reveal?
Immunology is already one of the most promising and rapidly advancing areas of medical science, with the potential to transform how we prevent and treat an enormous range of diseases.
Immunotherapy has already produced breakthrough treatments for cancers including melanoma, lung cancer, leukemia and lymphoma. Now scientists are exploring how the immune system can be harnessed against Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s and many other devastating conditions.
This is about investing in a broad scientific field that touches most of the diseases that kill and disable millions of Americans.
Prop. 38 gives qualified scientists and researchers the ability to determine which projects show the greatest scientific promise within that field.
And California is uniquely positioned to lead. We have many of the world’s leading universities, scientists and research institutions. Prop. 38 gives them the stable funding and shared infrastructure to turn scientific promise into treatments and cures.
What oversight mechanisms are in place to ensure the money is spent responsibly?
Prop. 38 limits state administrative costs to no more than 2%, requires all grant funds to public universities and nonprofit research centers be spent directly on medical research, implements rigorous conflict of interest rules, requires public disclosure of all spending, and mandates independent financial audits. Funds can only be granted to California-based nonprofit universities and research institutes, and no funds can be given to for-profit corporations.
For the distribution of the competitive grants, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will organize a 7-member executive committee of appointees from the University of California campuses with the most qualified research facilities, including: Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco.
Additionally, treatments and technologies resulting from the research generally must be available here at prices at least 20% below the national average.
The bottom line is simple: Every dollar is traceable, accountable and focused on advancing research to save lives.
What do opponents get most wrong about this measure?
They lose sight of what Prop. 38 is actually about: saving lives.
Millions of Californians who are dealing with devastating diseases cannot afford to wait while promising medical research stalls because federal funding is being cut or because scientists lack the resources they need.
Prop. 38 creates a collaborative network of California universities, nonprofit research institutions and scientists focused on accelerating breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to save millions of lives.
It cultivates a world-class immunology research institute serving as a “hub” to foster collaboration among public universities, nonprofit research institutions and researchers. Requirements help ensure the institute is truly first-in-class globally, with the resources, expertise, staff, facilities, medical technology, information technology and access to clinical trials, patients and medical facilities to accelerate cures.
Prop. 38 will create something California has never had before: a permanent, collaborative research ecosystem that combines competitive funding with a world-class institution designed to create cures that save lives.
What did we miss? What should we have asked you?
The impact on patients.
Imagine a new treatment that gives someone with cancer another decade with their family. An Alzheimer’s therapy that allows a parent to recognize their own children longer. Or a therapy that prevents a devastating disease before a family ever has to confront it.
That is the promise behind Prop. 38.
California is home to many of the greatest scientists, universities and research institutions in the world. Prop. 38 gives them stable, long-term funding and a statewide network to collaborate and move promising discoveries from the laboratory to patients faster.
That’s why leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others support Prop. 38.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 3:39 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:06 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
Why should Californians vote against funding research that could cure cancer or Alzheimer’s?
We strongly support biomedical research, including research on cancer and Alzheimer’s disease. The question is not whether the science is worthwhile, but whether Proposition 38 is a responsible way to fund it. It is not.
The measure would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, repayment would cost the General Fund more than $12 billion or about $500-600 million annually for 20 years. Those payments would compete with health care, education, public health, housing and other essential services.
Prop. 38 would also commit an extraordinary sum to immunology and immunotherapy while excluding hundreds of other important research priorities. California can support excellent science without allowing a ballot campaign to determine scientific priorities for a generation.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
The state could potentially get a return on its investment through revenue sharing. Isn’t that a smart financial move?
The possibility of revenue isn’t a repayment plan. The promised financial return is uncertain in both size and timing. Prop. 38 requires 10% of revenue generated by funded discoveries to be returned to the state. Most basic discoveries, however, never become commercial products, and those that do commonly require years of additional research, clinical trials, regulatory review, manufacturing and private investment.
California’s experience with stem-cell research illustrates the risk of promising that research bonds will pay for themselves. The original stem-cell program authorized $3 billion in bonds, with a substantially larger repayment cost after interest. Its royalty returns have been modest relative to that public investment. Prop. 38 uses a different revenue-sharing formula, but speculative future income should not be treated as a dependable source of bond repayment.
The principal return from biomedical research is better health and scientific knowledge. Those benefits can be enormous, but they should not be confused with a guaranteed financial return to the state treasury.
We hope the research pays off — for patients and taxpayers alike. But a possible payoff isn’t a repayment plan.
Without this bond, how should California ensure it remains a leader in medical innovation?
California is already an international leader in biomedical research. In fiscal year 2025, four California institutions ranked among the nation’s 15 largest recipients among more than 2,500 institutions that receive National Institutes of Health funding: University of California, San Francisco, Stanford, UC San Diego and UCLA. University of Southern California, UC Davis, UC Irvine, Scripps Research, UC Berkeley and many other institutions also have exceptional research programs.
California should build on that strength through transparent, statewide competition. If the state chooses to supplement federal funding, it could create a broadly mandated research program that uses independent peer review, regularly reassesses priorities, and allows all qualified institutions and fields to compete. Scientific opportunities change rapidly; a sound funding system should be able to change with them.
Doesn’t the 20% discount on treatments provide a direct, tangible benefit to California residents?
A 20% discount would be welcome if an effective treatment emerged, but the provision is narrower and less certain than it sounds. It applies only to treatments resulting from Prop. 38-funded research and sold in California. Most funded projects will not produce a marketable therapy, and successful products could take many years to reach patients.
While the discount may sound attractive, forcing lower prices for California may incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled. The consequence could even be shortages in the state that developed the new approaches.
The measure also leaves unanswered questions about how the discount would be calculated, enforced and coordinated with insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, federal programs and confidential rebates. A promised discount on treatments that may never reach patients does not justify more than $8 billion in borrowing and decades of taxpayer repayments.
Twenty percent off an unknown price, for a treatment that may never arrive, is hardly a guarantee of affordable care.
How do you respond to the argument that federal funding cuts make state-level investments like this necessary?
The NIH has consistently enjoyed strong support from both Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. Congress. The president’s 2026-2027 budget included sharp cuts for the NIH and related research agencies. But Congress restored most of the funding. This is not to say we are satisfied with the federal outlook. We clearly support increased federal investment in biomedical research. Further, we find the politicization of the funding process unacceptable. Products of publicly funded research are available to anyone in any state or country. It is admirable that California might want to backfill some of the budget cuts. But, we feel, the costs should be shared equally among recipients of the benefit. That is why we believe in supporting a strong federal effort.
Medical breakthroughs benefit the whole country. Paying for them should be a shared national responsibility.

This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready?
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)
